insights.view: 此人事变动凸显零售业对时尚买手和品类管理经验的重视。对FMCG感官研究而言，意味着需更关注跨品类人才带来的消费者洞察方法融合，以及时尚趋势对快消品感官体验的潜在影响。
insights.action: 建议CMI团队关注零售高管变动背后的品类策略信号，并评估时尚零售的感官营销实践是否可借鉴于快消品，如门店体验与产品触感优化。

readings.title: The world is whiffing on its biggest climate goal
body: Today, Explained newsletter The world is whiffing on its biggest climate goal So where, exactly, does the climate fight go next? by Caitlin Dewey Sep 2, 2026, 9:05 PM UTC Gift Even as we strive to limit climate change, we need to brace for the warming we can no longer prevent. Neil Milton/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images Caitlin Dewey is a senior writer and editor at Vox, where she helms the Today, Explained newsletter. This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day. Subscribe here . For more than a decade, 1.5 degrees Celsius has been the watchword — er, watch temperature? — of climate policy. If the world could hold warming at that level, it could stave off some of climate change’s worst effects, researchers believed. Well…there’s bad news on that front. A major new assessment from the United Nations concludes the world will inevitably pass the 1.5-degree benchmark within the next few years, barring some celestial intervention. Under current policies, we’re on track to hit 2.6 degrees of warming between now and 2100. And while that’s not quite a Mad Max scenario, it will very much change how humans live. (More on that in just a minute!) Email (required) Sign Up By submitting your email, you agree to our Terms and Privacy Notice . This site is protected by reCAPTCHA and the Google Privacy Policy and Terms of Service apply. In many ways, the new report formalizes what researchers and policymakers have warned for years . Last November, UN Secretary-General António Guterres made international headlines when he acknowledged that a “temporary overshoot” of 1.5 degrees was “inevitable.” People understandably fixated on that “inevitable” bit. But “temporary” matters, too. As this new assessment repeatedly stresses, the efforts we make now to cut emissions and remove carbon from the atmosphere will still ultimately determine the size and duration of the much-feared “overshoot.” The realities of a rapidly warming world also point to a second, equally urgent task: Even as we strive to limit climate change, we need to brace for the warming we can no longer prevent. That approach, known as “climate adaptation,” has not always been popular among advocates or philanthropists. Adaptation is “a kind of laziness, an arrogant faith in our ability to react in time to save our skins,” Al Gore wrote in his 1992 book Earth in the Balance . Gore has since changed his tune, however, and so have many others. Among the most prominent converts is the billionaire philanthropist Bill Gates, who has gradually made adaptation a larger piece of his climate agenda. Last October, Gates released a controversial memo arguing that climate policy should measure success by improvements in human welfare “even more than” changes in emissions or temperature. But there’s no reason we can’t advance both goals together. Many countries and US states already have, in fact. After a 2003 heat wave killed roughly 15,000 people in France, the country created a “robust” national heat plan that included early warnings and checks on vulnerable residents. The system is credited with making subsequent heat waves less deadly (although a historic heat wave earlier this summer still caused 5,700 excess deaths ). Other adaptations will be far more disruptive. Fiji, for instance, has begun relocating coastal villages threatened by rising sea levels. And whatever adjustments society makes, life in a warming world will still be more difficult and more expensive. Maybe that’s why “climate adaptation” no longer sounds like laziness: There is clearly no easy or low-effort way out of all of this. ➨ Beware the “loneliness economy.” A booming cottage industry of paid apps, meet-ups, and clubs promise they can make you friends …for a fee. But many of these products and services do little more than sell the idea of community. Did you know ...Iran is the only country that has a legal market for selling kidneys ? Economists believe that creating similar markets elsewhere could help reduce the shortage of transplantable organs, but the idea is morally repugnant in many cultures. Today’s trivia: What iconic, long-standing web portal uses a butterfly logo? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword . Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: Yesterday we asked you for the flower that the Aztecs believed could attract the souls of the dead. That would be the marigold , which is still a mainstay of Day of the Dead ofrendas and celebrations. ##段落
《今日解说》通讯  
全球正与最重大的气候目标失之交臂  
那么，气候斗争下一步究竟该走向何方？  
作者：凯特琳·杜威  
2026年9月2日，晚上9:05 UTC  
赠阅  

即便我们努力限制气候变化，仍需为无法再阻止的变暖做好准备。  
尼尔·米尔顿/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images  

凯特琳·杜威是Vox的高级撰稿人和编辑，负责主持《今日解说》通讯。本文首发于《今日解说》——一份每日通讯，帮助你理解当天最引人注目的新闻与故事。在此订阅。

##段落
十多年来，1.5摄氏度一直是气候政策的关键词——呃，关键温度？研究人员曾认为，如果全球能将升温控制在这一水平，就能避免气候变化带来的一些最严重后果。  
嗯……这方面有个坏消息。  
联合国一项重要新评估得出结论：除非有上天干预，否则世界将在未来几年内不可避免地突破1.5摄氏度的门槛。按照现行政策，从现在到2100年，我们正走向升温2.6摄氏度的轨道。虽然这还不至于变成《疯狂麦克斯》式的末日景象，但必将深刻改变人类的生存方式。（稍后详谈！）

##段落
电子邮件（必填）  
注册  
提交邮箱即表示你同意我们的条款和隐私声明。本网站受reCAPTCHA保护，并适用谷歌隐私政策和服务条款。

##段落
从许多方面来看，这份新报告只是正式确认了研究人员和政策制定者多年来一直发出的警告。去年11月，联合国秘书长安东尼奥·古特雷斯承认1.5摄氏度的“暂时超标”是“不可避免的”，此事成为国际头条新闻。人们理所当然地聚焦于“不可避免”这几个字。  
但“暂时”同样重要。正如这份新评估反复强调的那样，我们现在为减排和从大气中去除碳所做的努力，最终仍将决定那个令人恐惧的“超标”的规模和持续时间。

##段落
快速变暖的世界所带来的现实，也指向了第二个同样紧迫的任务：即便我们努力限制气候变化，仍需为无法再阻止的变暖做好准备。  
这种方法被称为“气候适应”，在倡导者和慈善家中并不总是受欢迎。阿尔·戈尔在1992年出版的《平衡中的地球》一书中写道，适应是“一种懒惰，是对我们能够及时反应以自救能力的傲慢自信”。  
不过，戈尔后来改变了态度，许多其他人也是如此。其中最著名的转变者之一是亿万富翁慈善家比尔·盖茨，他已逐步将适应纳入其气候议程的更大版图。去年10月，盖茨发布了一份颇具争议的备忘录，主张气候政策应以人类福祉的改善来衡量成功

##段落
福利“甚至超过”排放或温度的变化。但没有理由我们不能同时推进这两个目标。事实上，许多国家和美国州已经做到了。2003年法国一场热浪造成约1.5万人死亡后，该国制定了一项“强有力的”国家高温应对计划，包括早期预警和对易受伤害居民的巡查。该体系被认为使随后的热浪致死率降低（尽管今年夏初的历史性热浪仍导致5700例超额死亡）。其他适应措施将更具颠覆性。例如，斐济已开始搬迁受海平面上升威胁的沿海村庄。无论社会做出何种调整，变暖世界中的生活仍将更加艰难和昂贵。也许这就是为什么“气候适应”不再听起来像懒惰：显然没有轻松或低成本的出路能解决这一切。

readings.title: 3 strategies for effective leadership, from a former astronaut
body: 3 strategies for effective leadership, from a former astronaut
" data-large-file="https://ideas.ted.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2023/11/IDEAS_Leadership_FINAL.jpg?w=770" /> Maria Petrishina / iStock

While there are various approaches to leading a team, many of us land on common questions in the search for an effective leadership style: How can I be there for my team? Do I need to command respect, or earn it? And the most crucial question of all: How can I make sure that my team trusts me?

Cady Coleman has been confronting these questions throughout her career as a chemist, engineer, Air Force colonel and astronaut. In conversation with TED science curator David Biello, Coleman shared three strategies to establish — and maintain — trust in a leader. Whatever your career is, these tips can help you to prepare your team to face any challenge you come across — in outer space or here on Earth.
People often say, “There’s no ‘I’ in team” … But maybe there should be.
1. Be brave enough to get to know your team members as individuals

People often say, “There’s no ‘I’ in team”… But maybe there should be, says Coleman. Every member of your team is a whole person, and since so many of the problems we face at work are interdisciplinary, understanding who each individual is beyond the 9-to-5 is valuable. Being vulnerable enough to get to know your team this way is an essential skill for any leader.

When you are able to say, “I think your world is different from mine, and I’d like to understand more about it,” you’re not just building trust; you’re opening a communication channel that teaches you more about your teammate’s qualities, says Coleman. This type of conversation requires the willingness and bravery to be vulnerable. Once you know what everyone brings to the table, you can foster the growth of qualities that can lead the team to collective success.

For example, as Coleman prepared for life on the space station, her advisors warned that the long periods of time away from family might be too much to handle. For her, however, this wasn’t a problem — she had been commuting and working away from her family for more than a decade. After sharing her experience, her colleagues realized she’d not only be adaptable to life on the space station, but also she could help others cope with the change, too.
2. Create a culture that’s open to everyone’s ideas
While leaders have to guide their teams, it’s equally important to let everyone know that they can advocate for themselves and bring their own ideas to the table.

Coleman benefitted from such leadership at NASA when she was training to go to the space station. In the face of budget cuts, NASA announced that they’d be eliminating their smaller space suits, meaning that if someone wasn’t qualified to use a larger space suit, they couldn’t go to the space station. This presented a choice for Coleman: wait for NASA to acquire suits that fit her or figure out how she could train in the larger suits. By working with NASA’s decision makers, Coleman was able to shift her training to use the bigger suits. Had she not felt the freedom to speak up, she says, she would have been waiting 10 years to go to the space station in a small suit.
When you make trust-building a central goal, the rest falls into place more easily.

Sometimes establishing trust in the workplace can be more difficult than you expect, but when you make trust-building a central goal, the rest falls into place more easily. Workplace dynamics are always changing — maybe a teammate’s work/life priorities have shifted, or a big mistake requires you all to work together under new pressures. These challenges make fostering trust tricky, but they are also moments of opportunity.

If a new challenge has arisen or trust has been breached, Coleman reminds us to “always figure out the why and the what.” Make sure to ask: why has this happened, why do they feel this way, and what can be done about it? Be open to different points of view, and don’t give up if you don’t get through at first. Connection is often in the smaller things you do; talk about food or music, write a note to compliment an idea and ask to hear more. This level of connection and vulnerability may not seem intuitive at first, but as you make trust a core part of your mission, it becomes easy.

Trust, Coleman reminds us, is both given and earned. As a woman, she knew gaining the trust of some male colleagues might be extra challenging. Her approach was simple: she performed well and, with patience and persistence, learned her colleagues’ language and taught them hers. The challenges in gaining trust will always be there, but if you model vulnerability, openness and understanding for your team, you’ll find the rewards will always be there, too.

This post was adapted from a recent LinkedIn Live conversation with Cady Coleman, former NASA Astronaut and author of the forthcoming book, Sharing Space: An Astronaut’s Guide to Mission, Wonder, and Making Change , due out July 2024.

##段落
有效领导的3个策略，来自一位前宇航员
2023年12月4日
/
约瑟夫·德布赖恩
Facebook
X
LinkedIn
Reddit
WhatsApp
玛丽亚·彼得里希娜 / iStock
" data-large-file="https://ideas.ted.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2023/11/IDEAS_Leadership_FINAL.jpg?w=770" /> 玛丽亚·彼得里希娜 / iStock
领导力是什么样子？
尽管领导团队的方法多种多样，但许多人在寻找有效领导风格时都会遇到一些常见问题：我如何支持我的团队？我需要命令别人尊重，还是赢得尊重？而最关键的问题是：我如何确保团队信任我？
凯迪·科尔曼在作为化学家、工程师、空军上校和宇航员的职业生涯中，一直在面对这些问题。在与TED科学策展人大卫·比耶洛的对话中，科尔曼分享了建立并维持领导者信任的三种策略。无论你的职业是什么，这些建议都能帮助你让团队准备好面对你遇到的任何挑战——无论是在外太空还是在地球上。
人们常说，“团队里没有‘我’”……但也许应该有。

##段落
1. 勇敢地去了解每个团队成员作为个体的特质
人们常说，“团队里没有‘我’”，但也许应该有，科尔曼说。你团队中的每个成员都是一个完整的人，而由于我们在工作中遇到的许多问题都是跨学科的，了解每个人在朝九晚五之外是谁非常有价值。以足够脆弱的心态去这样了解你的团队，是任何领导者的必备技能。
科尔曼说，当你能说“我觉得你的世界和我的不同，我想了解更多”时，你不仅在建立信任，还在打开一条沟通渠道，让你更了解队友的品质。这种对话需要愿意并勇敢地展现脆弱。一旦你知道每个人能带来什么，你就能培养那些能引领团队取得集体成功的品质。
例如，当科尔曼为空间站生活做准备时，她的顾问警告说，长时间远离家人可能难以承受。然而，对她来说，这不是问题——她已经通勤并在远离家人的地方工作了十多年。在分享她的经历后，同事们意识到她不仅能适应空间站的生活，还能帮助其他人应对这种变化。

##段落
2. 营造一个对所有人想法都开放的文化
虽然领导者必须引导团队，但同样重要的是让每个人都知道他们可以为自己发声，并把自己的想法带到台面上。
科尔曼在NASA训练时受益于这种领导方式，当时她正在为前往太空站做准备。

面对预算削减，NASA宣布将淘汰较小的太空服，这意味着如果某人没有资格使用较大的太空服，他们就不能前往空间站。这对科尔曼来说是一个抉择：等待NASA获得适合她的太空服，或者想办法如何训练自己使用较大的太空服。通过与NASA的决策者合作，科尔曼得以调整训练，使用较大的太空服。她说，如果她没有感到可以自由发声，她可能要等上10年才能穿着小太空服前往空间站。

##段落
当你把建立信任作为核心目标时，其他事情就会更容易水到渠成。

##段落
3. 让信任成为你的使命

有时在工作场所建立信任可能比你预期的更困难，但当你把建立信任作为核心目标时，其他事情就会更容易水到渠成。职场动态总是在变化——也许队友的工作/生活优先事项发生了变化，或者一个大错误要求你们都在新的压力下共同工作。这些挑战使培养信任变得棘手，但它们也是机遇的时刻。

##段落
如果出现了新的挑战或信任被破坏，科尔曼提醒我们要“始终弄清楚原因和内容”。务必问：为什么会发生这种情况，他们为什么会有这样的感受，以及对此能做些什么？对不同观点保持开放态度，如果一开始没有达成共识，不要放弃。联系往往存在于你做的小事中；谈论食物或音乐，写张便条赞美一个想法并请求了解更多。这种程度的联系和脆弱性起初可能看起来不直观，但随着你让信任成为使命的核心部分，它就会变得容易。

##段落
科尔曼提醒我们，信任既是给予的，也是赢得的。作为一名女性，她知道获得一些男性同事的信任可能格外具有挑战性。她的方法很简单：她表现出色，并以耐心和坚持，学会了同事们的语言，也教会了他们她的语言。赢得信任的挑战总是存在的，但如果你为团队树立脆弱性、开放性和理解的榜样，你会发现回报也总是存在的。

##段落
这篇文章改编自最近与凯迪·科尔曼的LinkedIn Live对话，她是前NASA宇航员，也是即将于2024年7月出版的《共享空间：宇航员关于使命、奇迹和变革的指南》一书的作者。

readings.title: How to look after your oral microbiome
body: 16 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Jasmin Fox-Skelly Your oral microbiome is the key to a healthy mouth and body. Here's how to make sure it's well-nourished. Everyone knows that sugary foods can lead to dental cavities, by feeding harmful bacteria in our mouths. But it turns out that keeping them away is as much about what you do eat as what you don't eat – and from fruit to cheese, the most beneficial foods might surprise you. Research is starting to uncover the importance of the oral microbiome. This community is made up of 700 different bacterial species , as well as viruses, fungi, and other microorganisms. It can have a profound effect on our health. Currently, though, it's often neglected. It doesn't have to be this way. It's easy to take care of your mouth microbes – and as with the gut, your diet is a major factor. Here's what you need to know to eat your way to healthy teeth.  In the bustling neighbourhood of your mouth, microbes carve out ecological niches, with each species preferring a distinct habitat . While some bacteria choose to inhabit the surface of teeth, others might prefer the tongue or lurk in the tiny crevices between your teeth and gums. Some of these microbes are bad news. Take Streptococcus mutans , which sits on the surface of teeth and loves to eat sugar. This bacterium turns sugars into acids that eat away at the protective enamel on teeth. Eventually this can lead to holes or cavities , which more than 80% of Americans have by the time they enter their mid-30s.  Other mouth microbes are actively helpful. For instance, if beneficial bacteria such as Veillonella, Actinomyces, some species of Streptococcus , or Neisseria make your mouth their home, they can prevent harmful pathogenic strains from colonising. Having a good oral microbiome isn't just important for dental health. If you don't brush your teeth regularly or fastidiously enough then small pockets can form in the space between teeth and gums. In this oxygen-poor environment, bugs such as Porphyromonas gingivalis can thrive. Once there, P. gingivalis causes gum disease, but also raises the risk of health problems such as cardiovascular disease , depression, Alzheimer's disease, diabetes , inflammatory bowel disease , rheumatoid arthritis , and even preterm birth . In recent years, scientists have increasingly linked a poor oral microbiome to colon and pancreatic cancer . In one recent study , a team of scientists from across the US tested the saliva of participants and then followed up to identify their subsequent risk of cancer. Those whose oral microbiome contained certain bacterial species linked to tooth decay or Candida yeast were found to have a higher risk of pancreatic cancer. There's also emerging evidence that, as with the gut, it's important to have a varied mix. For instance, one recent study found that a lower diversity of microbes in the mouth is associated with depression . But crucially, brushing your teeth alone is not enough to maintain this microbial community. Everything you eat, they eat – and this has a direct effect on which ones can thrive. Snacks or beverages to avoid are those primarily made up of lots of sugar, as these are gobbled up by cavity-causing bacteria. It's also a good idea to limit your intake of processed carbohydrates, as these are easily broken down into sugars in the mouth.  Starchy snacks to avoid include white bread, crackers, biscuits, cakes, and pretzels. Attracting "good" bacteria is helpful for two reasons. They compete for food and space with those that are linked to cavities and disease, reducing their populations. But some also directly attack the ones you don't want moving into your mouth. "Within the broader family of these sugar loving microbes, Streptococcus, there are some [bacteria] that don't produce much acid at all, and they'll actually attack some of the microbes that do produce acid," says Laura Weyrich, associate professor of anthropology and bioethics at Pennsylvania State University in the US, who studies the oral microbiome and how it has changed throughout history. "They're like freedom fighters – they have their own antibiotics that they use as weapons. So if you have these bacteria then you're going to be in good shape," says Weyrich. For example, the friendly bacteria S. salivarius produces proteins that can kill a wide variety of unwanted microbes. This includes pathogens with resistance to conventional antibiotics. If you want to cultivate a healthy oral microbiome, one of the best things you can do is eat plenty of leafy green vegetables. Foods such as kale, spinach, beetroot and radishes contain high amounts of nitrate, which is gobbled up by Neisseria bacteria in our mouths. The microbes convert this nitrate into nitrite, which is then further changed by bacteria in the gut into nitric acid. Nitric acid circulates in the blood and acts to reduce blood pressure, benefiting cardiovascular health. For instance, in one trial , older adults who drank nitrate rich beetroot juice twice a day for two weeks saw their blood pressure fall. Weirdly, chewing garlic – although it may not do wonders for your breath – can also benefit oral health, as it contains a chemical called allicin that attacks the bacteria that cause cavities and gum disease. Eating a largely plant-based diet can benefit your oral microbiome in other ways too. The reason is down to a class of compounds found in plants called polyphenols. When it gets too hot, cold, or sunny, animals can simply get up and move to a more hospitable environment. Plants don't have this luxury, so instead they produce polyphenols – special antioxidants that protect their cells and tissues from damage. More like this: •  How ultra-processed foods affect our gut microbiome •  Scientists are regrowing human teeth •  The best way to brush your teeth However, polyphenols can protect against harmful bacteria too. For instance, Wu's research and that of others has shown that the polyphenols found in tea can suppress the "bad" oral bacteria that cause cavities and gum disease and stop them from clumping together and attaching to the surface of teeth.   "The polyphenols inhibit one of the enzymes that is responsible for the stickiness of the plaque," says Christine Wu, professor of paediatric dentistry at the University of Illinois Chicago College of Dentistry in the US, whose research focuses on foods that could help combat oral pathogens. In Wu's study, drinking tea also appeared to inhibit the bacteria responsible for bad breath, which live at the back of the tongue. Other foods rich in polyphenols include many fruits, particularly dark-coloured berries. This is why, contrary to what you may expect, these sugar and acid-rich foods can benefit oral health. Wu's research has shown that drinking cranberry juice can prevent the growth of dental plaque, and inhibit the bacteria associated with cavities and periodontal disease. Honey is also packed with polyphenols and has likewise been shown to prevent plaque formation and fight against the bacteria that causes cavities. Chewing on cheese is also thought to have some benefits for our oral communities. In one small study by researchers in Italy, nine participants were asked to eat Grana Padano cheese each day for five days. At the end of the study, the scientists found that the genetic signatures of the bacterial communities in their mouths had shifted slightly, with fewer of the sugar-loving S. mutans and more S. sanguinis, a bacteria more likely to be found in healthy mouths. Cheese can also counteract some of the harm caused by S. mutans . "Cheese is awesome because it has all the good properties of milk, but it is solid, so when you chew it the saliva increases," says Wu. "The saliva will get rid of some of the extra sugar on the tooth or in the mouth, and because saliva is neutral it buffers the acid that's produced in the mouth." Fermented foods can also benefit your oral microbiome as they contain beneficial bacteria that compete with the "baddies." For instance a recent review found that drinking kefir – a fermented milk product – could inhibit certain oral pathogens and stop them from producing their sticky biofilm. However, according to Gaetano Isola, associate professor of periodontology at the University of Catania, Italy, there is no single "superfood" for oral health, and what matters much more is the overall dietary pattern.  "If we repeatedly consume refined sugars and easily fermentable carbohydrates, we favour microorganisms that are particularly efficient at producing and tolerating acids," he says. He explains that, over time, this can shift the microbial community towards an imbalance. "By contrast, an overall diet richer in whole plant foods, fibre and complex carbohydrates and lower in frequent refined-sugar exposure is more compatible with maintaining a stable oral ecosystem." A simple practical tip from Isola is to favour whole plant foods – vegetables, whole fruits, legumes and whole grains – rather than refined carbohydrates. A recent study in which Isola was involved found that people who adhered more closely to a Mediterranean-style diet, known for its emphasis on fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and healthy fats, tended to have less severe gum disease. Patients who did not follow the Mediterranean diet as closely tended to have more severe gum disease, especially if they consumed red meat frequently. It's not clear what might be causing the association between red meat and gum disease. One idea is that the protein may create an oral environment that favours harmful microbes, such as P. gingivalis. Of course, brushing and flossing is still essential. Flossing has been associated with lower concentrations of the dental pathogen S. mutans , while brushing the teeth and tongue significantly decreases microbes associated with dental diseases. Scientists don't yet know how regular over-the-counter mouthwashes affect your oral microbiome . The hope is that one day they could be used to balance microbial communities rather than just reducing the total amount of bacteria present. Some mouthwashes that contain chlorhexidine, on the other hand, are known to disrupt the balance of oral microbes. These can still help to treat gum disease and certain other oral conditions in the short term.  But for a healthier mouth microbiome, eating the right foods is a powerful tool in your arsenal.  "It's the same thing that everybody always says – which is kind of boring – which is sticking to a diet that's well balanced and has lots of vegetables, lots of leafy greens, lean proteins and limiting your sugar intake, especially sugary drinks," says Weyrich.  So why not make yourself a sumptuous salad, or a selection of fine cheeses washed down with a hot cup of tea. Not only will doing so benefit your body – you'll be making the good microbes in your mouth happy too. -- For trusted insights on health and wellbeing, sign up to the Health Fix newsletter by senior health correspondent Melissa Hogenboom who also writes the Live Well For Longer and Six Steps to Calm courses.   For more science, technology, environment and health stories from the BBC, follow us on Facebook and Instagram .  Health Bacteria Food Diet Mental health Features

16小时前 分享 保存 设为Google首选 Jasmin Fox-Skelly 你的口腔微生物组是健康口腔和身体的关键。以下是如何确保它得到良好滋养的方法。众所周知，含糖食物通过喂养口腔中的有害细菌，可能导致蛀牙。但事实证明，远离这些细菌不仅关乎你不吃什么，还关乎你吃什么——从水果到奶酪，最有益的食物可能会让你大吃一惊。研究开始揭示口腔微生物组的重要性。这个群落由700种不同的细菌物种，以及病毒、真菌和其他微生物组成。它对我们的健康有着深远的影响。然而，目前它常常被忽视。这种情况并非不可避免。照顾口腔微生物很容易——就像肠道一样，饮食是一个主要因素。以下是你需要知道的，通过饮食获得健康牙齿的方法。 在你口腔的繁忙社区中，微生物开辟出生态位，每个物种偏好不同的栖息地。虽然一些细菌选择居住在牙齿表面，但其他细菌可能偏好舌头或潜伏在牙齿和牙龈之间的微小缝隙中。其中一些微生物是坏消息。以变形链球菌为例，它附着在牙齿表面，喜欢吃糖。这种细菌将糖转化为酸，侵蚀牙齿的保护性牙釉质。最终，这可能导致蛀洞或龋洞，超过80%的美国人在35岁左右时都有这样的问题。 其他口腔微生物则积极有益。例如，如果有益细菌如韦荣球菌、放线菌、某些链球菌或奈瑟菌在你的口腔中安家，它们可以防止有害致病菌株的定植。拥有良好的口腔微生物组不仅对牙齿健康重要。如果你没有定期或彻底刷牙，牙齿和牙龈之间的空间可能会形成小袋。在这个缺氧环境中，像牙龈卟啉单胞菌这样的细菌可以繁衍生息。一旦存在，牙龈卟啉单胞菌会导致牙龈疾病，但也增加健康问题的风险，如心血管疾病、抑郁症、阿尔茨海默病、糖尿病、炎症性肠病、类风湿性关节炎，甚至早产。近年来，科学家越来越将不良口腔微生物组与结肠癌和胰腺癌联系起来。在一项近期研究中，来自美国各地的科学家团队测试了参与者的唾液，然后进行随访以确定他们随后的癌症风险。那些口腔微生物组中含有与蛀牙或念珠菌酵母相关的特定细菌物种的人，被发现患胰腺癌的风险更高。还有新兴证据表明，像肠道一样，重要的是

保持口腔微生物的多样化组合非常重要。例如，最近一项研究发现，口腔中微生物多样性较低与抑郁症相关。但关键在于，仅靠刷牙并不足以维持这一微生物群落。你吃的每一口食物，它们也在吃——这直接影响哪些微生物能够繁衍生息。应避免的零食或饮品主要是那些含糖量高的，因为这些糖分会被致龋细菌迅速吞噬。同时，限制加工碳水化合物的摄入也是个好主意，因为它们在口腔中容易分解成糖。应避免的淀粉类零食包括白面包、饼干、酥饼、蛋糕和椒盐卷饼。

吸引“好”细菌之所以有益，有两个原因。它们与致龋和致病相关的细菌争夺食物和空间，从而减少后者的数量。而且，有些好细菌还会直接攻击那些你不想让它们进入口腔的细菌。“在嗜糖微生物的大家族链球菌中，有些细菌几乎不产酸，它们实际上会攻击那些产酸的微生物，”美国宾夕法尼亚州立大学研究口腔微生物组及其历史变迁的人类学与生物伦理学副教授劳拉·韦里奇说。“它们就像自由斗士——拥有自己的抗生素作为武器。所以，如果你拥有这些细菌，你的口腔状况就会很好，”韦里奇表示。例如，友好的唾液链球菌会产生蛋白质，能杀死多种有害微生物，包括对常规抗生素具有耐药性的病原体。

如果你想培养健康的口腔微生物组，你能做的最好的事情之一就是多吃绿叶蔬菜。羽衣甘蓝、菠菜、甜菜根和萝卜等食物含有大量硝酸盐，这些硝酸盐会被口腔中的奈瑟菌吞噬。这些微生物将硝酸盐转化为亚硝酸盐，后者再由肠道中的细菌进一步转化为一氧化氮。一氧化氮在血液中循环，有助于降低血压，促进心血管健康。例如，在一项试验中，老年人每天喝两次富含硝酸盐的甜菜根汁，持续两周，血压有所下降。奇怪的是，咀嚼大蒜——虽然可能对口气没什么神奇效果——也能有益口腔健康，因为它含有一种叫做大蒜素的化学物质，能攻击导致蛀牙和牙龈疾病的细菌。

以植物为主的饮食还能以其他方式有益于你的口腔微生物组。其原因归结于植物中发现的一类化合物，称为多酚。当天气变得太热、太冷或阳光太强时，动物可以站起来移动到更适宜的环境。植物却没有这种能力。

这种奢侈的保护方式，因此它们转而产生多酚——这是一种特殊的抗氧化剂，能保护植物细胞和组织免受损伤。更多类似内容：• 超加工食品如何影响我们的肠道微生物组 • 科学家正在重新生长人类牙齿 • 刷牙的最佳方式 然而，多酚也能抵御有害细菌。例如，吴博士及其他人的研究表明，茶叶中发现的多酚可以抑制导致蛀牙和牙龈疾病的“坏”口腔细菌，并阻止它们聚集在一起附着在牙齿表面。 “多酚能抑制一种负责牙菌斑黏性的酶，”美国伊利诺伊大学芝加哥分校牙科学院的小儿牙科教授克里斯汀·吴说，她的研究重点是可能有助于对抗口腔病原体的食物。在吴的研究中，饮用茶似乎也能抑制生活在舌头后部、导致口臭的细菌。其他富含多酚的食物包括许多水果，特别是深色浆果。这就是为什么，与你可能预期的相反，这些富含糖和酸的食物反而有益于口腔健康。吴的研究表明，饮用蔓越莓汁可以防止牙菌斑的生长，并抑制与蛀牙和牙周病相关的细菌。蜂蜜也富含多酚，并且同样已被证明能防止牙菌斑形成，对抗导致蛀牙的细菌。咀嚼奶酪也被认为对口腔微生物群落有一些益处。在一项由意大利研究人员进行的小型研究中，九名参与者被要求连续五天每天食用帕达诺奶酪。研究结束时，科学家发现他们口腔中细菌群落的基因特征发生了轻微变化，嗜糖的变形链球菌减少，而更多的血液链球菌（一种更常见于健康口腔的细菌）出现。奶酪还能抵消变形链球菌造成的一些损害。“奶酪很棒，因为它拥有牛奶的所有优点，但它是固体的，所以当你咀嚼时唾液会增加，”吴说。“唾液会清除牙齿上或口腔中的一些多余糖分，而且因为唾液是中性的，它能缓冲口腔中产生的酸。”发酵食品也有益于口腔微生物组，因为它们含有与“坏细菌”竞争的有益细菌。例如，最近的一项综述发现，饮用开菲尔（一种发酵乳制品）可以抑制某些口腔病原体，并阻止它们产生黏性生物膜。然而，根据意大利卡塔尼亚大学牙周病学副教授加埃塔诺·伊索拉的说法，没有单一的口腔健康“超级食物”，而

更重要的是整体饮食模式。“如果我们反复摄入精制糖和易发酵的碳水化合物，就会偏爱那些特别擅长产生和耐受酸的微生物，”他说。他解释说，随着时间的推移，这可能会使微生物群落转向失衡状态。“相比之下，整体饮食中富含全植物性食物、纤维和复杂碳水化合物，而较少频繁接触精制糖，更有利于维持稳定的口腔生态系统。”伊索拉提供的一个简单实用建议是，优先选择全植物性食物——如蔬菜、完整水果、豆类和全谷物——而非精制碳水化合物。最近一项伊索拉参与的研究发现，更严格遵循地中海式饮食（以强调水果、蔬菜、全谷物和健康脂肪著称）的人，往往牙龈疾病严重程度较低。那些不严格遵循地中海饮食的患者，牙龈疾病往往更严重，尤其是如果他们经常食用红肉。目前尚不清楚红肉与牙龈疾病之间关联的具体原因。一种观点认为，红肉中的蛋白质可能创造一个有利于有害微生物（如牙龈卟啉单胞菌）生长的口腔环境。当然，刷牙和使用牙线仍然至关重要。使用牙线与降低牙科病原体变形链球菌的浓度相关，而刷牙和刷舌则能显著减少与牙科疾病相关的微生物。科学家目前尚不清楚常规非处方漱口水如何影响口腔微生物组。他们希望未来有一天，漱口水能用于平衡微生物群落，而不仅仅是减少细菌总数。另一方面，一些含有氯己定的漱口水已知会破坏口腔微生物的平衡。这些产品在短期内仍有助于治疗牙龈疾病和某些其他口腔问题。但为了更健康的口腔微生物组，摄入正确的食物是你武器库中的有力工具。“这正是大家常说的——虽然有点老生常谈——即坚持均衡饮食，富含大量蔬菜、绿叶蔬菜、瘦肉蛋白，并限制糖分摄入，尤其是含糖饮料，”韦里奇说。那么，何不为自己准备一份丰盛的沙拉，或精选几种优质奶酪，配上一杯热茶呢？这样做不仅有益于你的身体——还能让你口腔中的有益微生物感到愉悦。——如需获取关于健康和福祉的可靠见解，请订阅资深健康记者梅丽莎·霍根布姆撰写的《健康修复》通讯，她还开设了《活得更久更健康》和《平静六步法》课程。如需更多科学、技术、环境和健康故事，请继续关注我们。

来自BBC的报道，欢迎在Facebook和Instagram上关注我们。健康 细菌 食品 饮食 心理健康 专题

readings.title: Why are more Americans moving to Ireland?
body: 15 April 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google Anne Cassidy In a historic reversal, the number of Americans moving to Ireland last year was higher than the number of Irish people migrating to the US. Was this just a blip or the start of a more profound trend? Michael Sable is an American stand-up comedian and communications manager who moved from Washington DC to Dublin in 2016.  Sable, who draws on his experience of being an American living in the Republic of Ireland in his stand-up routine, says that, when he first arrived, many Irish people he met were surprised he'd made the move, but now they don't question it.  "I've noticed that, as the years go on, people have been less and less incredulous when hearing that an American moved to Ireland," he says.  Sable is one of a rising number of people who have moved to Ireland from the US, with the latest data showing the figure nearly doubling from  4,900 to 9,600 between 2024 and 2025 ,  exceeding the number of Irish people headed in the opposite direction.   It comes as the US saw more people leave than arrive last year, according to a report from US think tank the  Brookings Institution . It said this was the first time that this had been the case "in at least half a century".  The think tank highlighted "dramatic changes in immigration policy" under the second administration of President Trump, including more removals of undocumented foreign workers, and the White House "all but suspend[ing]" the US programme for accepting refugees.    Separately, more American citizens are choosing to move abroad than ever before, says the  Wall Street Journal.  It calculated that "at least 180,000 Americans" voluntarily left the US in 2025, which it said was a record high.   The reversal in the flow of migration between Ireland and the US marks a historic turning point in the shared history of the two countries, which have deep-rooted ties.  For centuries, millions of Irish people emigrated to the US in search of work or a better life, making Irish Americans one of the country's largest ethnic groups. There have been several US presidents with Irish ancestry, including John F Kennedy and Joe Biden, whose visits to Ireland were  celebrated more like homecomings  than diplomatic missions.   Irish writer Colm Tóibín has frequently explored the relationship between Ireland and the US in his work, particularly in his novels, Brooklyn and Long Island, which follow the story of an Irish girl who emigrates to America in the 1950s.  Tóibín, who lives in the US, says the relationship between the US and Ireland has changed. "A myth was created that America was a great place of opportunity and wealth," he says. "It was built into the [Irish] culture that if there's any trouble, you go to England, if there's any ambition or spark you go to America." "The flow of young people [from Ireland to the US] looking for work just hasn't continued. So, that is going to be a big change in the future, because you're not going to get the same easy connection between Ireland and America," he adds.  The trend partly reflects political shifts in both countries. As well as developing into a high-tech, export-driven knowledge economy, Ireland has undergone a social transformation in recent decades, moving from a deeply conservative society to a liberal, progressive nation, following referendums on divorce, abortion and gay marriage.    Tóibín, who was a prominent campaigner for the "yes" vote in Ireland’s same-sex marriage referendum, says: "Everyone became more aware that Ireland was a more liberal, cosmopolitan, open society, and that it would be a good place to live." By contrast, the US has moved to the political right under President Trump, who, since returning to office, has launched a major crackdown on illegal immigration.   Tóibín revisits the Irish-American immigrant experience in his latest short story collection, The News from Dublin. In one story in the collection, Five Bridges, the protagonist is an undocumented Irish immigrant preparing to leave America before US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, known as Ice, come looking for him. The number of Irish citizens deported from the US  rose by more than 50%  in 2025.  "There are large numbers of Irish people in America who are official in every way – they pay taxes, own their own house, have kids in school, but they came in on a tourist visa," says Tóibín. "If Ice found them, Ice would detain them. That's really frightening." Expatsi, a firm that helps US citizens to move abroad,  reported it experienced a month's worth of traffic  in the hours after President Trump's election in 2024. Expatsi co-founder Jen Barnett says the reasons Americans cite for leaving are wide-ranging. "[Factors include] what's going on politically in the US, and has been for 10 years, the cost of living, and then safety. Gun violence is so prevalent," she says.  Politics was also a driving factor for Kevin Wozniak, an American lecturer living in Ireland. He and his husband left Boston in 2023 after he got a post at Maynooth University, 23km (14 miles) west of Dublin.  "My motivation to look at opportunities abroad was deep fears about the trajectory of the country in the era of Donald Trump," Wozniak says. "Ireland has liberalised very significantly and has moved in exactly the opposite direction that the US is moving." Natalia Lange, a migrant support worker based in Crosshaven, county Cork, moved there from Michigan with her husband after the 2024 US election. Lange, who is half-Hungarian and has an EU passport, dreamed of living in Ireland since visiting on a school trip. "Politically, Ireland aligns much more with how we think," she says. "The US has the infrastructure to take in a lot more people, but it's a lot less inviting." Lauren Udoh, from Houston, Texas, moved to Claregalway, in county Galway, in 2021 after marrying her Irish husband. Udoh, who has two young children, works as an executive assistant and documents expat life on social media under the moniker TheGalwayGal.  "One of the biggest benefits is safety. I feel a lot safer here," she says. "With kids going to school, you don’t have to worry about school shootings." Emigration from Ireland has fallen, with 65,600 people leaving in the year to April 2025, a  6% decrease on 2024 , according to the Irish Central Statistics Office (CSO). For those wanting to live abroad, Australia is the most popular destination.  The CSO said 13,500 people left Ireland for Australia in the year to April 2025, the highest level since 2013. This is more than double the estimated 6,100 people who left Ireland for the US, which was, however, still up 22% on the previous year.   Restrictions around J1 visas, which allow Irish university students to work and travel in the US, has caused many  Irish students to rethink studying in the US.    Karen McHugh, CEO at Safe Home Ireland, an organisation supporting Irish-born emigrants wishing to return to Ireland, says: "We've certainly noticed an increase in queries about returning [from the US to Ireland]," she says. "Australia and Canada are two major countries where people are now going to from Ireland, and that's ease of getting a visa." Irish student Jamie McElhinney is currently on a work placement in Portugal as part of his hospitality management course. McElhinney, who studies at Dundalk Institute of Technology, says current immigration controls put him off seeking a work placement in the US. "I was going to go to Boston, and then all of the news about Ice started coming out. It’s a deterrent from going over there," he says.  While there are opportunities in Ireland, with  employment at 74.4%,  there is also a growing housing crisis, with recent  protests  over the shortage of affordable housing.  Barnett says the housing shortage is something the Americans her company helps to relocate are mindful of, adding: "They don't want to add to [the housing crisis], so one of the things we talk to them about is staying out of city centres." Sable, whose Irish grandparents emigrated to the US in 1939, is one of many Americans whose ancestry enabled them to get an Irish passport. Applications for Irish passports in the US rose by 10% in 2024 , the Irish Department of Foreign Affairs reported.  Sable now thinks of Ireland as home. "Culturally, I identify a lot more with Irish people," he says. "It's a very collective society, not huge on individualism like in the US." More like this:  •  Why Ireland's film industry is booming    •  Is New York's cannabis business flying high?   •  The 'brutal' toll of war on Dubai’s tourist trade Bill Hillyard, another American with Irish roots, relocated to Ireland for the cooler climate. He and his wife Anne left California following wildfires in 2019. "My wife said we need to move somewhere where it rains." They now run a pub called The Algiers in Baltimore, Co Cork.  Hillyard says he now tries to avoid turbulent events in the US. "I tried not to follow the news because I'm here now," he says. "But I'm reminded every day, because everyone asks me about Trump and what's going on there… I'm West Cork's ambassador to the US at this point." -- For global insights and expert analysis for the boardroom and beyond, sign up to the  World of Business newsletter , while  The Essential List  delivers a handpicked selection of features and insights. For more on business and beyond, follow us on  LinkedIn . Business Migration Features World of Business

2026年4月15日 分享 保存 设为谷歌首选 安妮·卡西迪 在一项历史性逆转中，去年从美国移居爱尔兰的人数超过了从爱尔兰移居美国的人数。这只是一次短暂波动，还是更深层次趋势的开端？迈克尔·萨布尔是一位美国单口喜剧演员兼传播经理，他于2016年从华盛顿特区搬到了都柏林。萨布尔在单口喜剧中融入了自己作为美国人在爱尔兰共和国生活的经历，他说，刚到达时，他遇到的许多爱尔兰人都对他的搬迁感到惊讶，但现在他们不再质疑了。“我注意到，随着时间推移，人们听到美国人搬到爱尔兰时，越来越少感到难以置信，”他说。萨布尔是越来越多从美国移居爱尔兰的人之一，最新数据显示，2024年至2025年间，这一数字从4900人几乎翻倍至9600人，超过了反向流动的爱尔兰人数量。与此同时，根据美国智库布鲁金斯学会的一份报告，去年美国离境人数超过了入境人数。报告称，这是“至少半个世纪以来”首次出现这种情况。该智库强调了特朗普总统第二任期内“移民政策的剧烈变化”，包括更多驱逐无证外国工人，以及白宫“几乎暂停”了美国难民接收计划。另外，《华尔街日报》称，选择移居海外的美国公民比以往任何时候都多。该报计算，2025年“至少有18万美国人”自愿离开美国，并称这是历史新高。爱尔兰与美国之间移民流动的逆转，标志着两国深厚历史渊源中的一个历史性转折点。几个世纪以来，数百万爱尔兰人移居美国寻找工作或更好的生活，使爱尔兰裔美国人成为该国最大的族群之一。多位美国总统拥有爱尔兰血统，包括约翰·F·肯尼迪和乔·拜登，他们对爱尔兰的访问更像归乡而非外交使命，受到热烈庆祝。爱尔兰作家科尔姆·托宾在其作品中频繁探讨爱尔兰与美国的关系，尤其是在他的小说《布鲁克林》和《长岛》中，这两部作品讲述了一个爱尔兰女孩在20世纪50年代移居美国的故事。居住在美国的托宾表示，美国与爱尔兰的关系已经改变。“曾有一个神话，说美国是充满机遇和财富的伟大之地，”他说，“这已融入爱尔兰文化中：如果遇到麻烦，就去英格兰；如果有雄心壮志，就去美国。”

##段落
或者激发你去美国。"从爱尔兰到美国寻找工作的年轻人流动已经不再持续。所以，这将在未来成为一个巨大的变化，因为你不会再得到爱尔兰和美国之间那种轻松的连接，"他补充道。这一趋势部分反映了两国的政治转变。除了发展成高科技、出口导向的知识经济外，爱尔兰近几十年来还经历了社会转型，在关于离婚、堕胎和同性婚姻的公投之后，从一个深度保守的社会转变为一个自由、进步的国家。

##段落
托宾曾是爱尔兰同性婚姻公投中"赞成"票的著名活动家，他说："每个人都更加意识到，爱尔兰是一个更自由、更国际化、更开放的社会，而且它会是一个宜居的好地方。"相比之下，美国在特朗普总统的领导下转向了政治右翼，特朗普自重返白宫以来，对非法移民发起了大规模打击。

##段落
托宾在他最新的短篇小说集《都柏林新闻》中重新审视了爱尔兰裔美国移民的经历。在该集的一个故事《五座桥》中，主角是一名无证爱尔兰移民，正准备在美国移民和海关执法局（俗称Ice）找上门之前离开美国。2025年，被美国驱逐出境的爱尔兰公民人数上升了超过50%。"在美国有大量爱尔兰人，他们在各方面都是合法的——他们纳税、拥有自己的房子、孩子在学校上学，但他们是持旅游签证入境的，"托宾说。"如果Ice找到他们，Ice会拘留他们。那真的很令人恐惧。"

##段落
帮助美国公民移居国外的公司Expatsi报告称，在2024年特朗普总统当选后的几个小时内，其网站流量就相当于平时一个月的量。Expatsi联合创始人詹·巴内特表示，美国人引述的离开原因多种多样。"（因素包括）美国国内的政治状况，而且这种情况已经持续了十年，生活成本，然后是安全问题。枪支暴力如此普遍，"她说。

##段落
政治也是居住爱尔兰的美国讲师凯文·沃兹尼亚克的一个驱动因素。2023年，他在都柏林以西23公里（14英里）的梅努斯大学获得职位后，他和丈夫离开了波士顿。"我寻找海外机会的动力，是对唐纳德·特朗普时代国家走向的深深恐惧，"沃兹尼亚克说。"爱尔兰已经非常显著地自由化了，而且其发展方向与美国完全相反。"

##段落
娜塔莉亚·朗格是驻扎在科克郡克罗斯哈文的移民支持工作者，她在2024年美国总统大选后与丈夫从密歇根搬到那里。朗格有一半匈牙利血统，持有欧盟护照，她梦想着住在爱尔兰，啜

##段落
一次学校旅行后，她萌生了这个想法。“在政治上，爱尔兰更符合我们的思维方式，”她说，“美国有基础设施接纳更多人，但那里不那么欢迎人。”来自得克萨斯州休斯顿的劳伦·乌多于2021年嫁给爱尔兰丈夫后，搬到了戈尔韦郡的克莱尔戈尔韦。乌多有两个年幼的孩子，担任行政助理，并以TheGalwayGal的网名在社交媒体上记录外籍生活。“最大的好处之一是安全。我在这里感觉安全得多，”她说，“孩子上学时，你不用担心中学校园枪击事件。”

##段落
根据爱尔兰中央统计局的数据，爱尔兰的移民流出已有所下降，截至2025年4月的一年中有65,600人离开，比2024年减少了6%。对于那些想居住在国外的人来说，澳大利亚是最受欢迎的目的地。统计局称，截至2025年4月的一年中，有13,500人从爱尔兰前往澳大利亚，这是自2013年以来的最高水平。这一数字是前往美国的约6,100人的两倍多，但前往美国的人数仍比上一年增长了22%。

##段落
J1签证允许爱尔兰大学生在美国工作和旅行，但相关限制已导致许多爱尔兰学生重新考虑赴美学习。支持爱尔兰出生侨民回国的组织Safe Home Ireland的首席执行官凯伦·麦克休说：“我们确实注意到有关从美国回国的咨询有所增加，”她说，“澳大利亚和加拿大是爱尔兰人现在前往的两个主要国家，这得益于签证办理的便利。”

##段落
爱尔兰学生杰米·麦克尔希尼目前在葡萄牙进行酒店管理课程的实习。麦克尔希尼就读于邓多克理工学院，他表示当前的移民管控让他不愿在美国寻找实习机会。“我本来打算去波士顿，但后来关于移民执法局的所有新闻都出来了。这让人不敢去那边，”他说。

##段落
尽管爱尔兰有就业机会，就业率达74.4%，但住房危机也在加剧，最近因经济适用房短缺爆发了抗议活动。巴尼特表示，她公司协助搬迁的美国人对住房短缺问题很在意，并补充说：“他们不想加剧住房危机，所以我们跟他们讨论的一个问题就是避开市中心。”塞布尔的爱尔兰祖父母于1939年移民美国，他是众多凭借血统获得爱尔兰护照的美国人之一。爱尔兰外交部报告称，2024年美国申请爱尔兰护照的人数增长了10%。塞布尔现在把爱尔兰视为家乡。“在文化上，我对爱尔兰人的认同感更强，”他说，“这是一个非常温

集体社会，不像美国那样强调个人主义。"更多类似内容：  
• 为什么爱尔兰电影业蓬勃发展  
• 纽约的大麻生意是否蒸蒸日上？  
• 战争对迪拜旅游业的“残酷”影响  

另一位有爱尔兰血统的美国人比尔·希利亚德（Bill Hillyard），因气候更凉爽而移居爱尔兰。他和妻子安妮（Anne）在2019年加州野火后离开了那里。“我妻子说我们需要搬到一个下雨的地方。”他们现在在科克郡（Co Cork）的巴尔的摩经营一家名为“阿尔及尔”（The Algiers）的酒吧。希利亚德说，他现在尽量避开美国的动荡事件。“我试着不关注新闻，因为我现在在这里，”他说，“但我每天都会被提醒，因为每个人都问我关于特朗普的事以及那边的情况……我现在算是西科克驻美国的大使了。”

readings.title: Inside a quest to learn about the ocean’s mysterious “deep reefs”
body: The Highlight Inside a quest to learn about the ocean’s mysterious “deep reefs” ﻿A decade ago, scientists left underwater structures in Palau. I was there when they went back for them. by Byrd Pinkerton Sep 1, 2026, 10:00 AM UTC Gift An autonomous reef monitoring structure (ARMS) in the mesophotic zone. | ﻿© Luiz Rocha Byrd Pinkerton is a host and senior correspondent on Unexplainable, Vox’s science podcast. She covers everything scientists don’t yet know but are trying to figure out, so her work explores everything from the inner workings of the human body to the distant edges of the universe . PALAU, Micronesia — On a bright, sunny day last May, I stood on a boat surrounded by the turquoise waters of the island nation of Palau. I was there in the western Pacific watching scuba divers as they prepared to bring up evidence of a mysterious aquatic world. Palau is famous for its spectacular and rich coral reefs. But these divers were planning to descend past those sun-lit marine communities and down into a lesser-known twilight zone known as the “mesophotic coral ecosystems.” A boat full of divers prepares to retrieve research structures from down in the “deep reefs.” Byrd Pinkerton/Vox Mesophotic essentially means “middle” and “light,” which is where these ecosystems are — not quite in the bright daylight, not quite in the profound darkness, but somewhere in between. For simplicity’s sake, we’ll call these communities, which range from some 30 meters to 150 meters below the surface, the “deep reefs.” Susanne Bähr, postdoc at the California Academy of Sciences, and Luiz Rocha, curator of Ichthyology at the California Academy, prepare their diving gear. Byrd Pinkerton/Vox One of the divers on the boat with me was a zoologist and curator at the California Academy of Sciences named Luiz Rocha, who has spent decades studying these deep reefs and their secrets. “Anything between 30 meters and 150 meters is really, really unknown,” he told me. Because these deep reefs are so unknown, researchers like Rocha are left with big questions. They want to get a baseline picture of what is going on in these ecosystems — even just who lives there! — so that they can better understand how they function. They’ve also tried to work out whether ( or not ) these deep reefs might provide a refuge for species living in shallower coral reefs. I was in Palau for Vox’s Unexplainable podcast because, in an effort to gather more information about these mysterious places, Rocha left some scientific structures down in these twilight depths back in 2016. Those structures then spent almost a decade becoming encrusted with all kinds of marine life. And now, Rocha was back to retrieve them, hoping that he — along with many other scientists — would be able to open them up, like a box of scientific puzzle pieces, full of clues about this under-understood marine world. One thing that’s often acknowledged in papers about and descriptions of the “mesophotic coral ecosystems” is that scientists don’t know as much as they’d like to. A National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration article about them from 2019 is full of “may’s” as in: they may “serve as essential fish habitat for economically and ecologically important species.” Researchers do know some things, of course. They know that these deep reefs can be found in many of the same locations as shallower coral reefs — so mainly the tropical and subtropical parts of the world, like Micronesia , the Caribbean , and even the Gulf of Mexico . They’ve found that there are many species that seem to be unique to these places, and recent research points to their potential susceptibility to climate change . In his work, Luiz Rocha wants to answer seemingly fundamental questions, among them: What is the main energy source for everything down here in the dimmer light? What does the food chain look like? How have things evolved to live down at these depths? © Luiz Rocha Researchers have also gotten a sense of some of the key differences between these deep reefs and their shallower coral neighbors. In shallow reefs, hard corals team up with photosynthesizing algaes . The algaes provide the corals with nutrients, and the corals secrete a calcium-carbonate matrix that helps create the architecture of the reef. As you go deeper, though, the light begins to fade, and the opportunities for photosynthesis start to fade with it. The temperature also drops. So the animals living down in the deep reefs are the ones that can survive in a dimmer, cooler world. Scientists can dive into the deep reefs to try to learn more about these understudied places — as Rocha has — but exploring down at 100 meters requires more difficult, riskier technical diving than exploring at shallower depths. The deeper you dive, for example, the faster gasses get pushed into your tissues, which imposes limits on these really deep dives. “We have a very, very short time,” Rocha says, “And by short time, I mean five minutes. Six, seven minutes.” Scientists might take some pictures in that time, or make some measurements, or collect a few samples, but then they have to move back upwards, a process which can take hours because they have to rise slowly to avoid decompression sickness. Previous Next It is, obviously, not particularly efficient to study an ecosystem in five- to seven-minute bursts. People have also used remote operated vehicles and submersibles to explore the deep reefs, but those have their own issues, and cameras can’t always capture all the detail you might want, or photograph more secretive, cryptic animals. So huge gaps remain in scientific knowledge about these ecosystems. “Whenever we go somewhere,” Rocha says, “the first thing we find is new species. … It’s the most basic thing in science you can do.” But this effort goes beyond just cataloguing new species of fish or sponges or sea slugs. Rocha wants to answer seemingly fundamental questions like: What is the main energy source for everything down here in the dimmer light? What does the food chain look like? How have things evolved to live down at these depths? How similar are they to the shallow ecosystems, and how different? How are they affected by climate change — and what’s the most efficient way to protect them? But, “in some ways we don’t even know what questions to ask,” Rocha says. “We really only know what questions to ask after we have a baseline understanding of what the ecosystem is. And for deep reefs, we don’t know that yet.” Rocha is not deterred by the enormous number of question marks that surround these deep reefs. For years now, he has been gathering bits of basic information about them, often via those very short dives. About a decade ago, though, Rocha got interested in another method for sampling the biodiversity of this sort of marine ecosystem — a technique involving “ autonomous reef monitoring structures ” (ARMS). Basically, each ARMS is a stack of several PVC plates, separated at uniform intervals and attached to a base plate. They look like little grey, featureless hotels. You take them to a place that you want to study, bring them down, secure them, and then leave them alone for a while to let them collect…life. In the bottom left corner, there is an ARMS encrusted with life. © Steve Lindfield “As soon as you drop any kind of clean structure on a reef,” Rocha says, “it starts getting colonized by larvae of everything around it — of sponges, gorgonians, corals. And then, because there’s all a lot of hiding spots between the plates — so between the floors of the hotel — they start getting colonized by shrimp, by mollusks, by ascidians, by anything you can imagine in the ocean. … And it becomes this stable, diverse mini reef, if you will, packed with a lot of biodiversity that would be very hard to collect all at once in any given reef.” A few years after that initial drop, you come back, collect the ARMS, and then study the mini reef that has grown on them. You can sample and touch and analyze things to your heart’s content. It’s not only a very effective way to collect lots of creatures, all at once, but also a great way to do so in a standardized way. If you went down — or sent a robot down — to collect an encrusted rock from a reef, you could learn a lot about the life on it, but it would be hard to compare the life on that rock to life on other rocks from other reefs, or even the same reef, because each rock would have its own unique characteristics. Not so for ARMS. “ Every one’s the same,” Chris Meyer, director of the Smithsonian Global ARMS program, told me, “It’s prefab housing, and then you just look to see who moves in.” Deep divers would descend down to find and retrieve the ARMS. They’d put the structures in a clear tub to keep organisms from being lost or washed away. The ARMS would be passed up, relay style, to shallower divers, and brought up to a boat full of scientists who were ready to receive them. © Susanne Bähr To Rocha, this seemed like a great way to get a really good, long look at the deep reefs instead of the brief glimpses he was getting from diving. It was also, he told me, fairly cheap to deploy them. So from 2016 to 2018, with some private funding, he and his colleagues left ARMS in some of the deep reefs around Palau — as well as in Guam, the Marshall Islands, and French Polynesia. They installed some around 50 meters, and some around 100, and then some around 10 meters, so he could compare the deep reefs to their shallower neighbors. After that, he waited. In fact, he waited a little longer than he would have liked, because the retrieval of ARMS is more expensive than deploying them, so he had to work out more funding. Eventually, private funders agreed to underwrite the retrieval of the ARMS that Rocha had left. Which is how he and his fellow divers finally found themselves on a boat in Palau again, ready to pull up these structures for the deep. Over the course of a few days, I watched a whole team of people pull several ARMS out of the deep reefs of Palau. Some of the ARMS were relatively sparse, but others were almost fuzzy with organisms — vibrant with red and orange and green and pink and white. One had a massive sponge attached to it, another had several delicate fronds dangling from it like coralline ferns. The ARMS collected each day traveled to the Palau International Coral Reef Center in bins full of seawater, where the scientists quickly got to work — seeing and touching (and smelling) this mysterious ecosystem right up close. Previous Next The process was, as it turned out, equal parts magical excitement and well-oiled, Cheez-It fueled disassembly line. After the plates were taken apart, Meyer took photographs of the plates — what he called a “time capsule of the place.” Others in the lab picked carefully through trays of debris, hunting for tiny crabs and worms and mollusks, or scraped samples off the plates and deposited them in tubes. They collected sea squirts, said to be our closest invertebrate relatives . They collected sponges — flat ones that felt dry underwater, thick ones with bristles like tiny, unmoving caterpillars, one as thin as a flake of skin and shot through with silver filaments. They collected strange, soft corals known as “octocorals,” and they collected colonies of animals called bryozoans, which created what looked like swirling, two-dimensional honeycombs. Previous Next “We’re looking for every unique thing, which we call a morphospecies,” a Smithsonian research biologist named Sarah Tweedt explained. “And we’re trying to get some representative tissue samples from all of these things so that we can sequence the DNA — and match the DNA to the organism.” That is, of course, assuming there is already a known genetic match in our existing DNA libraries. Byrd Pinkerton/Vox On the first day that I spent with the team, a Cal Academy curator named Terry Goslinger identified several potential new species. He is an expert on colorful, delightful sea slugs known as nudibranchs, and so, because of his deep knowledge (and because nudibranchs’ bright hues and patterns make them somewhat easier to tell apart than some other underwater creatures), he was able to make some on-the-spot calls about whether or not certain species were likely to be new to science, pending genetic testing to confirm. Previous Next Many of the animals were trickier to pin down, though. The researchers did their best to identify the creatures they were finding, but even now, several months out, there’s still a lot of work to be done. Of the close to 3,000 specimens, only a small fraction were identified at a species level. The numbers are a little bit inexact because researchers are still processing the data, but when I checked in with a Cal Academy postdoc working on the project, Susanne Bähr, in July, she told me that only 3 percent of samples had been ID’d by species, and a little less than 20 had a genus designation. Many, many more were only identified at higher, broader taxonomic levels. Genetic testing of the samples, paired with photographs and descriptions of the samples, will help people work out more specific species, and also help them identify whether certain species are new to science. At the end of the identification process, the material left on the plates was scraped off with a paint scraper, ground up in a blender, and squeezed dry in a process one researcher called “milking the turd.” The “turd” of material can then also be sampled for DNA, to work out what else might have been down there in the deep. Byrd Pinkerton/Vox The most important parts of this work will involve more than just identifying species. In fact, the more time I spent with these researchers in the lab, (including one evening spent with them as they worked past midnight), the more I got the sense that, while they seemed excited about seeing new species, they seemed equally excited to witness relationships between animals. The researchers working late into the night. Byrd Pinkerton/Vox When I walked into the lab one day, for example, several people urged me to go over and look through a microscope at a creature known as a pompom crab — a tiny yellow crustacean holding purple anemones in its modified front claws. Tweedt was extremely jazzed when she found something referred to as a “skeleton shrimp,” which looked to me like the marine equivalent of a stick insect, blending in on something called a hydroid. She pulled me aside another time, around one in the morning, to show me “the frosting on the cake” of the day, which turned out to be some bright red sea snails and the bright red octocorals they seemed to live on As she put it in a later conversation, these relationships are, in many ways, the key takeaway from this ARMS project, and what distinguishes it from efforts to bring up a few individual samples at a time. Studying them, or even just looking at the fuller picture ARMS provide, is what will let researchers tackle some of the outstanding questions about these ecosystems. Bähr, for example, is already working with the data from ARMS retrieved in Guam, trying to analyze how much overlap (or lack thereof) there is between species at different depths in the deep reefs. Really, though, this is all just the beginning. In one of our conversations, Rocha compared the work they are doing now to ecology work done in the mid-20th century to understand how species’ vertical distribution changes as you go up a mountain. This drove home for me how far behind researchers working on the mesophotic deep reefs are compared to their colleagues working on, say, shallower coral reefs. I asked him what kept him working on such a difficult puzzle. “It’s the reward at the end of it,” he said, “If it’s a hard puzzle, at the end of it, the reward is always bigger.” “But…in our lifetimes, will we assemble the deep reef puzzle?” I asked. “No, we will not assemble the puzzle, no,” Rocha said, “but we’ll generate some good pieces for the next generation to assemble.” One last plate before we go. ##段落
在探寻海洋神秘“深层珊瑚礁”的旅程中，十年前，科学家们在帕劳留下了水下结构。当它们被回收时，我恰在现场。作者：Byrd Pinkerton，2026年9月1日，上午10:00 UTC。一张自主珊瑚礁监测结构（ARMS）在中光层区域的照片。| © Luiz Rocha

##段落
Byrd Pinkerton是Vox科学播客Unexplainable的主持人和资深记者。她报道所有科学家尚未知晓但正试图解答的内容，因此她的工作涉及从人体内部运作到宇宙遥远边缘的方方面面。密克罗尼西亚帕劳——去年五月一个阳光明媚的日子，我站在一艘船上，周围是岛国帕劳碧蓝的海水。我在西太平洋，观看水肺潜水员准备打捞一个神秘水下世界的证据。帕劳以其壮观且丰富的珊瑚礁而闻名，但这些潜水员计划下潜至阳光照射的海洋生物群落之下，进入一个鲜为人知的过渡带，即“中光层珊瑚生态系统”。

##段落
一船潜水员准备回收“深层珊瑚礁”中的研究结构。Byrd Pinkerton/Vox。中光层一词本质上意味着“中间”和“光线”，这正是这些生态系统的位置——既不在明亮的日光下，也不在完全的黑暗中，而是介于两者之间。为简化起见，我们将这些位于水面以下约30米至150米的群落称为“深层珊瑚礁”。加州科学院博士后Susanne Bähr和加州科学院鱼类学馆长Luiz Rocha正在准备他们的潜水装备。Byrd Pinkerton/Vox。

##段落
与我同船的一位潜水员是加州科学院的动物学家兼馆长Luiz Rocha，他花费数十年研究这些深层珊瑚礁及其秘密。“30米到150米之间的任何地方都极其未知，”他告诉我。由于这些深层珊瑚礁如此陌生，像Rocha这样的研究者面临巨大问题。他们希望获得这些生态系统状况的基线图像——甚至只是谁居住在那里！——以便更好地理解其运作方式。他们还试图确定这些深层珊瑚礁是否可能为较浅珊瑚礁中的物种提供庇护所。我因Vox的Unexplainable播客来到帕劳，因为为了收集这些神秘地点的更多信息，Rocha于2016年将这些科学结构留在了过渡带深处。这些结构随后在近十年间被各种海洋生物覆盖。现在，Rocha返回回收它们，希望他——以及许多其他科学家——能像打开一盒珍宝一样将它们开启。

这些科学拼图碎片充满了关于这个尚待了解的海洋世界的线索。在关于“中光层珊瑚生态系统”的论文和描述中，经常被承认的一点是，科学家们对其了解程度远不及他们所愿。美国国家海洋和大气管理局在2019年发布的一篇相关文章充满了“可能”一词，例如，它们可能“为经济和生态上重要的物种提供关键鱼类栖息地”。当然，研究人员确实知道一些事情。他们知道，这些深层珊瑚礁可以在许多与较浅珊瑚礁相同的地点找到——因此主要分布在世界的热带和亚热带地区，如密克罗尼西亚、加勒比海，甚至墨西哥湾。他们发现，有许多物种似乎是这些地方独有的，而最近的研究指出它们可能易受气候变化的影响。在他的工作中，Luiz Rocha想要回答一些看似基本的问题，其中包括：在这较暗的光线下，这里所有生物的主要能量来源是什么？食物链是什么样子？生物是如何进化到生活在这些深度的？

##段落
研究人员还对深层珊瑚礁与其较浅的珊瑚邻居之间的一些关键差异有所了解。在浅层珊瑚礁中，硬珊瑚与进行光合作用的藻类共生。藻类为珊瑚提供营养，而珊瑚则分泌一种碳酸钙基质，有助于构建珊瑚礁的结构。然而，随着深入水下，光线开始减弱，光合作用的机会也随之减少。温度也在下降。因此，生活在深层珊瑚礁中的动物是那些能够在更暗、更冷环境中生存的物种。科学家们可以潜入深层珊瑚礁以试图了解更多关于这些研究不足的地方——正如Rocha所做的那样——但在100米深处探索比在较浅深度探索需要更困难、风险更高的技术潜水。例如，潜水越深，气体被推入你组织的速度就越快，这对这些非常深的潜水施加了限制。“我们只有非常非常短的时间，”Rocha说，“而所谓短时间，我的意思是五分钟。六分钟，七分钟。”科学家们可能在那段时间里拍照、进行一些测量或收集一些样本，但随后他们必须向上移动，这个过程可能需要数小时，因为他们必须缓慢上升以避免减压病。

##段落
显然，以五分钟到七分钟的短暂爆发来研究一个生态系统并不是特别高效。人们也曾使用遥控潜水器和载人潜水器来探索深层珊瑚礁，但这些工具有其自身的问题，而且相机并不总能捕捉到你可能想要的所有细节，或者拍摄到更隐蔽、神秘的动物。因此，巨大的

关于这些生态系统，科学知识仍存在空白。“每当我们去某个地方，”罗查说，“首先发现的就是新物种……这是科学中最基本的事情。”但这项工作不仅仅是记录新种类的鱼、海绵或海参。罗查想回答看似基础的问题，比如：在光线更暗的深处，这里一切的主要能量来源是什么？食物链是什么样子？生物是如何进化到适应这些深度的？它们与浅层生态系统有多相似，又有多不同？它们如何受气候变化影响——以及保护它们的最有效方式是什么？然而，“在某种程度上，我们甚至不知道该问什么问题，”罗查说。“我们只有在基本了解生态系统是什么之后，才知道该问什么问题。而对于深礁，我们还不了解。”罗查并未被围绕这些深礁的无数问号所阻挠。多年来，他一直通过那些非常短暂的潜水收集关于它们的基本信息片段。不过，大约十年前，罗查对另一种采样这类海洋生态系统生物多样性的方法产生了兴趣——一种涉及“自主珊瑚礁监测结构”（ARMS）的技术。基本上，每个ARMS是由若干PVC板堆叠而成，以均匀间隔分开并连接到底板上。它们看起来像灰色、无特色的微型酒店。你把它带到想研究的地方，放入水中，固定好，然后放置一段时间，让它们收集……生命。在左下角，有一个布满生命的ARMS。© 史蒂夫·林德菲尔德“一旦你把任何干净的结构放到珊瑚礁上，”罗查说，“它就会开始被周围一切生物的幼虫定殖——海绵、柳珊瑚、珊瑚。然后，因为板之间有很多藏身之处——即酒店楼层之间——它们开始被虾、软体动物、海鞘以及你能想象到的海洋中任何生物定殖……它变成了一个稳定、多样化的微型珊瑚礁，充满了大量在任何特定珊瑚礁中很难一次性收集到的生物多样性。”初次投放几年后，你回来收集ARMS，然后研究其上生长的微型珊瑚礁。你可以随心所欲地采样、触摸和分析。这不仅是同时收集大量生物的有效方式，也是以标准化方式进行的好方法。如果你亲自下去——或派机器人下去——从珊瑚礁收集一块布满生物的岩石，你可以了解其上生命的许多情况，但很难将那块岩石上的生命与其他珊瑚礁上的其他岩石进行比较，甚至难以与同一珊瑚礁上的其他岩石比较。

在同一片礁石上，因为每块岩石都会有自己独特的特征。但ARMS并非如此。“每一个都是一样的，”史密森尼全球ARMS项目主任克里斯·迈耶告诉我，“这是预制住房，你只需看看谁搬进来了。”深潜员会下潜寻找并回收ARMS。他们会将结构体放入一个透明桶中，以防生物丢失或被冲走。ARMS会被以接力方式传递给较浅水域的潜水员，最终送到一艘满载准备接收的科学家船上。© Susanne Bähr 对罗查来说，这似乎是获得对深礁长期细致观察的好方法，而不是像潜水那样只能短暂一瞥。他还告诉我，部署它们的成本相当低。因此，从2016年到2018年，凭借一些私人资金，他和同事们在帕劳周围的深礁——以及关岛、马绍尔群岛和法属波利尼西亚——放置了ARMS。他们有些安装在约50米深，有些在约100米，还有些在约10米处，这样他就能将深礁与其较浅的邻近区域进行比较。之后，他等待了。事实上，他等待的时间比预期的要长，因为回收ARMS比部署更昂贵，所以他不得不筹集更多资金。最终，私人资助者同意支持罗查留下的ARMS的回收。这就是他和他的潜水伙伴们最终再次出现在帕劳一艘船上的原因，准备为深海将这些结构体拉上来。在几天的时间里，我看着整个团队从帕劳的深礁中拉出几个ARMS。有些ARMS相对稀疏，但其他几乎被生物覆盖，毛茸茸的——充满红色、橙色、绿色、粉色和白色的活力。一个上面附着巨大的海绵，另一个则悬挂着几片精致的叶片，像珊瑚藻蕨类。每天收集的ARMS被装在充满海水的大桶中运往帕劳国际珊瑚礁中心，科学家们迅速开始工作——近距离观看、触摸（甚至嗅闻）这个神秘的生态系统。整个过程，事实证明，既有神奇的兴奋感，也有运转顺畅、以奇滋饼干为动力的拆解流水线。板块拆开后，迈耶拍摄了板块照片——他称之为“这个地方的时间胶囊”。实验室里的其他人仔细挑选托盘中的碎屑，寻找微小的螃蟹、蠕虫和软体动物，或从板块上刮取样本放入试管中。他们收集了海鞘，据说是我们最亲近的无脊椎动物亲属。他们收集了海绵——有在水下感觉干燥的扁平种类，有带有像微小不动毛虫的刚毛的厚种类，还有薄如皮肤碎片且布满……

他们采集了银色的细丝，收集了被称为“八放珊瑚”的奇异软珊瑚，以及名为苔藓虫的动物群落，这些苔藓虫形成了看似旋转的二维蜂窝结构。上一页 下一页 “我们寻找每一种独特的东西，称之为‘形态种’，”史密森尼研究生物学家莎拉·特威德特解释说。“我们试图从所有这些生物中获取代表性的组织样本，以便进行DNA测序——并将DNA与生物体匹配。”当然，这假设在现有的DNA库中已有已知的基因匹配。Byrd Pinkerton/Vox 在我与团队共度的第一天，加州科学院馆长特里·戈斯林格识别出几种潜在的新物种。他是研究色彩缤纷、令人愉悦的裸鳃类海蛞蝓的专家，因此，凭借他的深厚知识（并且因为裸鳃类海蛞蝓的鲜艳色彩和图案使它们比其他一些水下生物更容易区分），他能够现场判断某些物种是否可能对科学界而言是新物种，有待基因检测确认。上一页 下一页 然而，许多动物更难确定。研究人员尽力识别他们发现的生物，但即使现在，几个月过去了，仍有大量工作要做。在接近3000个标本中，只有一小部分在物种层面被识别。数字略有不准，因为研究人员仍在处理数据，但当我7月联系该项目的加州科学院博士后苏珊·贝尔时，她告诉我只有3%的样本被识别到物种，略少于20%有属级分类。更多的样本仅在更高级、更广泛的分类层被识别。样本的基因检测，结合照片和样本描述，将帮助人们确定更具体的物种，也有助于判断某些物种是否对科学界为新发现。在识别过程结束时，板上留下的材料用油漆刮刀刮下，在搅拌机中磨碎，并挤干，这一过程被一位研究人员称为“挤奶粪便”。然后可以从“粪便”材料中采样DNA，以找出深海可能还有什么。Byrd Pinkerton/Vox 这项工作中最重要的部分不仅仅是识别物种。事实上，我与这些研究人员在实验室待的时间越长（包括一个晚上陪他们工作到午夜之后），我越感觉到，尽管他们对发现新物种感到兴奋，但他们对见证动物之间的关系也同样兴奋。研究人员工作到深夜

##段落 一天晚上。Byrd Pinkerton/Vox 有一天我走进实验室时，几个人催我过去通过显微镜看一种叫绒球蟹的生物——那是一种微小的黄色甲壳动物，它改造过的前爪里握着紫色海葵。Tweedt 发现一种被称为“骷髅虾”的东西时兴奋极了，在我眼里那就像海洋版的竹节虫，藏身于一种叫水螅的生物中。另一次大约凌晨一点，她把我拉到一边，给我看当天“蛋糕上的糖霜”，结果发现是一些亮红色的海螺，以及它们似乎赖以生存的亮红色八放珊瑚。正如她后来一次谈话中所说，这些关系在许多方面是 ARMS 项目的关键收获，也是它与一次只带回几个单独样本的努力的区别所在。研究它们，或者哪怕只是观察 ARMS 提供的更完整图景，都能让研究人员解决关于这些生态系统的一些悬而未决的问题。例如，Bähr 已经在处理从关岛回收的 ARMS 数据，试图分析深礁不同深度物种之间的重叠程度（或缺乏重叠）。不过，说真的，这一切只是开始。在我们的一次对话中，Rocha 把他们现在所做的工作比作 20 世纪中期研究物种垂直分布随登山高度变化的生态学工作。这让我深刻意识到，研究中光带深礁的研究人员与那些研究较浅珊瑚礁的同行相比，落后了多少。我问他是什么让他坚持研究这样一个难题。“是最后的回报，”他说，“如果是个难题，到最后，回报总是更大。”“但是……在我们有生之年，能拼好深礁这块拼图吗？”我问。“不，我们拼不完，”Rocha 说，“但我们会为下一代拼出一些好碎片。”在我们离开前，还有最后一块板块。Byrd Pinkerton/Vox 查看更多：气候 播客 科学 焦点 难以解释 一位联邦法官刚刚发现一种全新方式，让 ICE 凌驾于法律之上 用最新的 Vox 填字游戏放松一下大脑 最高法院最糟糕的想法之一，或许能从特朗普手中拯救中期选举 要真正阻止数据中心，需要什么？ 最高法院刚刚给了特朗普他的非法舞厅 邮箱（必填） 注册 提交邮箱即表示你同意我们的条款和隐私声明。本网站受 reCAPTCHA 保护，并适用 Google 隐私政策和服务条款。广告客户内容 来自 这是原生广告的标题

readings.title: 6 ways to give that aren’t about money
body: Good news: You can be a generous person without writing a bunch of checks. In fact, many of the most awe-inspiring and effective examples of generosity are gifts of time and energy, talent and love, custom-fitted to a specific need. This type of giving is open to everyone.
Many of the most awe-inspiring and effective examples of generosity are gifts of time and energy, talent and love, custom-fitted to a specific need.

Not sure where to begin? Here are six gifts of time and attention that have the strong potential to spark ripple effects that affect millions, from head of TED Chris Anderson’s new book, Infectious Generosity .

Zen master Thich Nhat Hanh taught that attention is the most precious gift we can give someone. This is where generosity starts — with a willingness to stop focusing on ourselves and to instead pay attention to someone else and their needs. From that act of connection, anything can happen.

Truth is, it can be difficult. We spend much of our time lost in our own worlds. We are often reluctant to focus on the issues that others are dealing with. So we put up shields. And that means that many of the people who could really use our attention never feel seen by us. The generosity of attention is therefore the generosity of being willing to be a little uncomfortable, to take down those shields, to give up some time, to risk coming to care about someone else.
Whether you stop and have a meaningful connection with a person in need or spend 30 minutes researching a cause you think might matter, you have already begun your generosity journey.

In our connected era, there’s a type of generosity that matters more than ever: a willingness to reach out to those with whom we disagree with. Many disputes today play out in public online. Huge audiences can become glued to online feuds. What if we could bring a satisfying resolution to more of these conflicts?

It’s hard to reach out to our critics. This is a particularly challenging form of the generosity mindset. You are sacrificing your personal comfort for the greater good of bringing people together. But if you’re successful, there’s a powerful knock-on benefit: You are helping change the tone of public discussion today. That’s a gift to all of us.
The single greatest gift we can give is knowledge — knowledge that solves a problem, fills a need or opens a pathway forward.
In countless circumstances, the single greatest gift we can give is knowledge — knowledge that solves a problem, fills a need or opens a pathway forward.

Our single biggest piece of advice to someone coming to speak on the TED stage is to think of their talk not as an opportunity to pitch something (like a business or a cause) but rather as a gift. It is a chance to freely share valuable ideas with the audience. And those ideas have the potential to impact a listener’s life for years to come.

If you possess knowledge that others may benefit from, consider how you could share it to create ripple effects. What may take you a few hours to prepare and act on could light up someone’s life — and that could just be the beginning.

In our connected age, the networks we have access to matter more than ever. Therefore, one of the most important forms of viral generosity is to help people connect with others. The simplest way to do this is to make an introduction.

As psychologist and TED speaker Adam Grant has argued, an introduction can be fairly easy to give — and unbelievably valuable to receive. Ask many people how they met their partner, got their dream job or found the perfect collaborator for their creative project, and the answer will often be the same: someone — a friend, a neighbor, a colleague — introduced them to the right person. What you’re effectively doing is giving someone else access to your network of resources. And those introductions can have exponential consequences.

In his remarkable book Human Universals , anthropologist Donald Brown documented how hospitality is one of hundreds of human behaviors that have been observed in every single culture ever studied. But if hospitality is so ubiquitous (and so pleasant), is it really a form of generosity? Well, yes. Quite apart from any costs involved, it takes effort to invite someone over, whether friends or possible future friends. It’s easier just to watch the next episode of the TV series you’re into.
So how can hospitality contribute to infectious generosity? Hospitality taps into our deepest instincts for connection to one another. And each experience of it evokes a desire to reciprocate.
People need money, food, shelter and healthcare, to be sure. But we also yearn for beauty, wonder, laughter, transcendence — all elements of enchantment.

Pioneering artist Lily Yeh was approached by the dancer and choreographer Arthur L. Hall to undertake a community art project in a derelict, abandoned plot in her home city of Philadelphia. “I was interested but totally scared,” Yeh recalled. “I had little resources and no experience in working outdoors in a community setting. I wanted to run away, but I did not want to see a coward in the mirror. So I stepped into the project.”

The community project became the Village of Arts and Humanities, an art park full of trees, sculptures and mosaics created by local adults and children in collaboration with Yeh. Yeh’s work led her to a profound realization: that creating beauty in public spaces is profoundly healing and transformative for communities.

People need money, food, shelter and healthcare, to be sure. But we also yearn for beauty, wonder, laughter, transcendence — all elements of enchantment. Those who can enchant can offer a gift of immense value.

6种不花钱的给予方式

好消息：你不必写下一堆支票，也能成为一个慷慨的人。事实上，许多最令人敬佩且最有效的慷慨之举，是量身定制地满足特定需求的时间与精力、才华与爱心的馈赠。这种给予方式对每个人开放。

##段落
许多最令人敬佩且最有效的慷慨之举，是量身定制地满足特定需求的时间与精力、才华与爱心的馈赠。

##段落
不知道从哪里开始？以下是六种时间与关注的馈赠，它们有巨大潜力激发影响数百万人的涟漪效应，摘自TED负责人克里斯·安德森的新书《传染性慷慨》。

##段落
1. 转移关注
禅宗大师一行禅师教导说，关注是我们能给予他人最珍贵的礼物。慷慨从这里开始——愿意停止关注自己，转而关注他人及其需求。从这种连接的行为出发，一切皆有可能。

##段落
事实上，这并不容易。我们大部分时间都迷失在自己的世界里。我们常常不愿去关注他人正在处理的问题。于是我们竖起盾牌。这意味着许多真正需要我们去关注的人，从未感受到被我们看见。因此，关注的慷慨，就是愿意让自己稍微不舒服、卸下那些盾牌、牺牲一些时间、冒险去在乎他人的慷慨。

##段落
无论你是停下来与需要帮助的人建立一次有意义的连接，还是花30分钟研究一个你认为可能重要的公益事业，你都已经开始了你的慷慨之旅。

##段落
2. 搭建桥梁
在我们这个互联的时代，有一种慷慨比以往任何时候都更重要：愿意主动接触那些与我们意见相左的人。如今许多争端都在线上公开上演。大量观众可能会痴迷于网络争斗。如果我们能为更多这样的冲突带来令人满意的解决，会怎样？

##段落
主动接触批评者很难。这是慷慨心态中极具挑战性的一种形式。你是在牺牲个人的舒适感，为了将人们凝聚在一起的更大福祉。但如果你成功了，会有一个强大的附带好处：你在帮助改变当今公共讨论的基调。这是送给所有人的礼物。

##段落
我们能给予的最大礼物是知识——能解决问题、满足需求或开辟前进道路的知识。

##段落
3. 分享知识
在无数情境中，我们能给予的最大礼物是知识——能解决问题、满足需求或开辟前进道路的知识。

##段落
我们对某人的最大建议是

在TED舞台上发言，要将其视为一份礼物，而非推销（如商业或事业）的机会。这是与听众自由分享宝贵想法的契机，而这些想法可能在未来多年影响听众的生活。
如果你拥有他人可能受益的知识，思考如何分享以产生涟漪效应。你花几小时准备和行动的内容，或许能点亮某人的生活——而这可能只是开始。
4. 促成联结
在这个互联时代，我们可接触的网络比以往更重要。因此，病毒式慷慨最重要的形式之一是帮助人们与他人建立联系。最简单的方式就是做介绍。
正如心理学家兼TED演讲者亚当·格兰特所言，介绍做起来相当容易——但对接受者来说却无比珍贵。问许多人如何遇见伴侣、获得梦想工作或找到创意项目的完美搭档，答案往往相同：有人——朋友、邻居或同事——把他们引荐给了对的人。你实际上是在让他人接触你的资源网络，而这些介绍可能产生指数级的影响。
5. 展现好客
在人类学家唐纳德·布朗的杰出著作《人类普遍性》中，他记录了热情好客是如何成为所有被研究文化中普遍观察到的人类行为之一。但如果好客如此普遍（且如此愉快），它真的算是一种慷慨吗？嗯，是的。撇开任何成本不谈，邀请某人来访——无论是朋友还是潜在的新朋友——都需要付出努力。而仅仅继续追看你喜欢的剧集则容易得多。
那么，好客如何促进传染性慷慨呢？好客触及我们与他人联结的最深层本能，而每一次体验都会唤起回报的渴望。
人们当然需要金钱、食物、住所和医疗保健，但我们也渴望美、惊奇、欢笑和超脱——这些都是迷醉的元素。
6. 创造迷醉
先锋艺术家莉莉·叶被舞蹈家兼编舞家亚瑟·L·霍尔邀请，在她的家乡费城一片废弃空地上开展社区艺术项目。“我感兴趣但完全害怕，”叶回忆道，“我资源匮乏，也没有在社区户外工作的经验。我想逃跑，但不想在镜子里看到懦夫，所以我踏入了这个项目。”
这个社区项目后来成为“艺术与人文之村”，一个充满树木、雕塑和马赛克的艺术公园，由当地成人和儿童共同创作。

##段落
与叶的合作让叶深刻认识到：在公共空间创造美，对社区具有深远的治愈和变革力量。
##段落
诚然，人们需要金钱、食物、住所和医疗保健。但我们也渴望美、惊奇、欢笑和超越——这些都是魅力的元素。能够带来魅力的人，可以给予一份极具价值的馈赠。
##段落

readings.title: The Pacific warming patterns warping US weather
body: 20 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Isabelle Gerretsen A rare but powerful combination of an immense Pacific Ocean heatwave and a "super El Niño" are set to have profound effects on US weather and marine life this autumn. Here are five changes to expect. In the north-east Pacific Ocean, an immense and persistent heatwave is wreaking havoc on marine life and weather patterns. "It's a really bright red eyeball in the Pacific," says Andrew Leising, a research oceanographer at the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa). "It's huge, it stretches across the whole [ocean]." The Pacific heatwave, which formed in May 2025, is already bringing surface temperatures 3-4C (5.4-7.2F) above average for this time of year, according to Leising. Add to that: a massive warming pattern known as El Niño is brewing further south. El Niño is a weather phenomenon that pushes up global temperatures, and it is also supercharging Pacific Ocean warming. It is expected to intensify this autumn to become the strongest El Niño in living memory . This combination of a massive marine heatwave and a "super El Niño" is rarely seen. Here are five impacts we can expect to see – and where they will happen. California: More storm surges, intense floods California, which has been in the grips of a marine heatwave since December, is bracing for more storm surges and flooding over the autumn and winter due to warmer coastal waters. Coastal water levels are already 15cm (5.9in) above mean sea level, says Patrick Barnard, research director of the Center for Coastal Climate Resilience at the University of California, Santa Cruz. During this El Niño, that already high sea level will soar further still: to at least 15-30cm (5.9-11.8in) higher than normal, says Barnard. "Every 5-10cm [1.9-3.9in] of mean sea level rise doubles the flooding frequency for most coastal communities along the US West Coast, so with all these expected sea level increases peaking this winter, we will have historically high flood risk," he says. Warmer ocean surfaces also evaporate more heat and moisture into the air, which can cause heavier rainfall, says Leising. This can lead to more atmospheric rivers – huge, invisible ribbons of water vapour in the sky – in the coming months. These raise the risk of heavy inland flooding and mudslides in California too. What is El Niño? El Niño is a natural phenomenon which occurs when sea surface temperatures in the Pacific Ocean are 0.5C (0.9F) higher than normal for several consecutive months. When the increase is 2C (3.6F), a "very strong" or "super" El Niño occurs.   Pacific Northwest US and Canada: Less snowfall, risk of drought Further north in the US and in Canada, the combined impact of El Niño and marine heatwaves is expected to reduce snowfall, says Larry O'Neill, professor at Oregon State University and director of the Oregon Climate Service. The last huge Pacific marine heatwave, coined "the Blob", led to a record low snowpack in the Pacific Northwest in 2015 . "It may have modified the jet stream and sent storms further north than usual. The storms we did get were much warmer than usual, so the precipitation that would usually come as snow came as rain at higher elevations," says O'Neill. Reduced snowfall is a concern as many parts of the Pacific Northwest are currently experiencing drought conditions , he adds. "It could take multiple winters for us to recover." Dry conditions and above-average warming in the north-west US, exacerbated by El Niño, increase the risk of wildfires across northern California, eastern Oregon, southern Idaho and Utah this autumn. This is projected to reduce air quality for millions and result in billions of dollars of economic impact. Meanwhile in California, warmer coastal waters have already led to warmer, more humid conditions across the state over the spring and summer this year, according to Leising. In inland California, temperatures also tend to be "a little warmer", during a marine heatwave, as the winds off the ocean pick up a little extra heat before moving away from the coast, says Nick Bond, a climatologist at the University of Washington.   Fewer Atlantic hurricanes, more Pacific storms Over in the Atlantic Ocean, El Niño tends to suppress hurricane development as it makes thunderstorms less likely to become hurricanes. But tropical storms in the eastern Pacific are stronger as warmer ocean waters provide additional energy, with heightened risk for Mexico. These tropical storms can help weaken marine heatwaves during the autumn, says O'Neill. "Evaporation from the winds and the cold temperatures tends to cool [them] off." A 2020 study by O'Neill found that strong storms fully destroyed marine heatwaves in the Northeast Pacific in a matter of days between 2013 and 2016. The heatwave off California is already "basically cooking the animals along the coast", says Leising. During a marine heatwave, nutrients don't rise to the ocean surface as often as they usually do and oxygen levels in the water are lower, says O'Neil. "A lot of fish and shellfish will not have enough oxygen, so they'll either die or they'll go further offshore." Fisheries are likely to feel the effects of this damage to the ecosystem, he says. The only marine heatwave to beat the current one for size led to "really big changes in the marine ecosystem" , says Bond. " The Blob ", which lasted from 2013-16, stretched for 1,000 miles (1,609km) between North America and Asia. "Warm water species thrived at the expense of the cooler water species," says Bond. This was detrimental for juvenile salmon, for marine mammals and some sea birds, he adds. The heatwave in the Pacific is starting to become more or less a permanent feature of the climate system – Nick Bond The duration of these heatwaves is a major concern, says Leising. "Marine animals will have been exposed to this warm water for a really long time over a large area, and now they're just going to roll right into the warm waters from El Niño." Some species, such as rockfish and squid, may benefit from warmer waters, "but overall the balance is more losers as the productivity is down for the whole system", he says. "There's less food out there for everyone." Large marine heatwaves have occurred each of the past seven years and six of these were  among the biggest on record for the eastern North Pacific since records began in 1982. The increase in these marine heatwaves is directly linked to climate change, says O'Neill. "Marine heatwaves are occurring more frequently now, because the ocean has been warming unrelentingly over the last 40 years."   More like this: •  The couple who married in typhoon floods •  How do you cool a 100F city? •  The most extreme hurricanes in history Since the 1970s, there has been a marked acceleration in sea surface temperatures and the ocean has absorbed more than 90% of the excess heat from climate change. Today, ocean temperatures are hotter than they have ever been . The heatwave in the northeast Pacific is "starting to become more or less a permanent feature of the climate system," says Bond. It is only the second time in recorded history that a marine heatwave of this magnitude has occurred alongside an El Niño, says Leising, noting that the relationship between these two events is not fully understood. Scientists are still working out how climate change influences El Niño , but agree that the frequency of these events is likely to increase this century due to global warming. Met Office forecasts suggest that sea surface temperature anomalies could exceed 3C (5.4F) later in 2026 as El Niño reaches its peak. El Niño events typically lasts 9-12 months , with this one expected to dissipate around spring. It is unknown how long the marine heatwaves will last. "They certainly do have some real persistence to them. The Blob had legs," says Bond. As long as the waters of the Pacific Ocean remain excessively hot, we can expect the weather and marine life to feel the effects. -- For essential climate news and hopeful developments to your inbox, sign up to the Future Earth newsletter, while The Essential List delivers a handpicked selection of features and insights twice a week. For more science, technology, environment and health stories from the BBC, follow us on Facebook and Instagram .
