##段落
20小时前 分享 保存 设为Google首选 伊莎贝尔·格雷特森 一场罕见而强烈的组合——广袤的太平洋海洋热浪加上“超级厄尔尼诺”——预计将在今年秋季对美国天气和海洋生物产生深远影响。以下是值得关注的五大变化。

##段落
在东北太平洋，一场巨大而持久的海洋热浪正在对海洋生物和天气模式造成严重破坏。“这是太平洋上一个极为醒目的红色眼球，”美国国家海洋和大气管理局（Noaa）的研究海洋学家安德鲁·莱辛说。“它规模巨大，横跨整个[海洋]。”据莱辛称，这场形成于2025年5月的太平洋热浪，已使海面温度比同期平均水平高出3-4摄氏度（5.4-7.2华氏度）。再加上：一种名为厄尔尼诺的大规模增温现象正在更南端酝酿。厄尔尼诺是一种推高全球气温的天气现象，同时也在加剧太平洋的变暖。预计它将在今年秋季增强，成为有生以来最强的厄尔尼诺。这种大规模海洋热浪与“超级厄尔尼诺”的组合极为罕见。以下是我们可以预期的五大影响——以及它们将发生的地点。

##段落
加利福尼亚州：更多风暴潮和严重洪水 自去年12月以来一直受海洋热浪影响的加利福尼亚州，由于沿海水域变暖，正为秋冬季节更多的风暴潮和洪水做好准备。加州大学圣克鲁兹分校沿海气候韧性研究中心研究主任帕特里克·巴纳德表示，沿海水位已比平均海平面高出15厘米（5.9英寸）。巴纳德说，在这次厄尔尼诺期间，本已偏高的海平面还将进一步攀升：至少比正常水平高出15-30厘米（5.9-11.8英寸）。“平均海平面每上升5-10厘米（1.9-3.9英寸），美国西海岸大多数沿海社区的洪水频率就会翻倍，因此随着所有这些预期的海平面上升在今年冬季达到峰值，我们将面临历史性的高洪水风险，”他说。莱辛还指出，较暖的海洋表面会向空气中蒸发更多热量和水分，这可能导致更强的降雨。这可能在接下来的几个月里引发更多大气河流——天空中巨大的、不可见的水汽带。这些也会增加加州内陆严重洪水和泥石流的风险。

##段落
什么是厄尔尼诺？ 厄尔尼诺是一种自然现象，当太平洋海面温度连续数月比正常水平高出0.5摄氏度（0.9华氏度）时发生。当增幅达到2摄氏度（3.6华氏度）时，就会出现“极强”或“超级”厄尔尼诺。

##段落
美国太平洋西北地区和加拿大：降雪减少，干旱风险增加 在美国更北部的地区和加拿大，厄尔尼诺与海洋热浪的叠加影响预计将减少降雪

俄勒冈州立大学教授兼俄勒冈气候服务处主任拉里·奥尼尔表示，上一次大规模太平洋海洋热浪被称为“斑点”，导致2015年太平洋西北地区积雪量创下历史新低。奥尼尔说：“它可能改变了急流，使风暴比平时更向北移动。我们遇到的风暴比平时温暖得多，因此通常以雪形式出现的降水在高海拔地区变成了雨。”他补充说，降雪减少令人担忧，因为太平洋西北部许多地区目前正经历干旱状况。“我们可能需要多个冬天才能恢复。”美国西北部的干燥条件和高于平均水平的变暖，加上厄尔尼诺现象的影响，增加了今年秋天北加州、俄勒冈州东部、爱达荷州南部和犹他州发生野火的风险。预计这将降低数百万人的空气质量，并造成数十亿美元的经济影响。与此同时，据莱辛称，在加州，今年春季和夏季，较温暖的沿海水域已经导致全州天气更加温暖潮湿。华盛顿大学气候学家尼克·邦德表示，在内陆加州，海洋热浪期间气温也往往“略高”，因为来自海洋的风在离开海岸前会吸收一些额外的热量。

更少的大西洋飓风，更多的太平洋风暴在大西洋，厄尔尼诺现象往往会抑制飓风的发展，因为它使雷暴不太可能变成飓风。但东太平洋的热带风暴更强，因为较温暖的海洋水域提供了额外的能量，墨西哥面临的风险更高。奥尼尔说，这些热带风暴可以在秋季帮助减弱海洋热浪。“风的蒸发和低温往往会使它们降温。”奥尼尔2020年的一项研究发现，在2013年至2016年间，强风暴在几天内完全摧毁了东北太平洋的海洋热浪。莱辛说，加州附近的海洋热浪已经在“基本上煮熟了沿海的动物”。奥尼尔说，在海洋热浪期间，营养物质上升到海洋表面的频率不如平时，水中的氧气含量也较低。“很多鱼类和贝类将没有足够的氧气，所以它们要么死亡，要么游到更远的近海。”他说，渔业可能会感受到这种生态系统破坏的影响。邦德说，唯一比目前规模更大的海洋热浪导致了“海洋生态系统的巨大变化”。“斑点”从2013年持续到2016年，在北美和亚洲之间绵延1000英里（1609公里）。邦德说：“温水物种以牺牲冷水物种为代价而繁盛。”这对

"或幼鲑鱼，对海洋哺乳动物和一些海鸟而言，他补充道。太平洋的热浪正开始或多或少成为气候系统的永久特征——尼克·邦德 这些热浪的持续时间是一个重大关切，莱辛说。“海洋动物将在很大范围内长时间暴露在这种温暖的水域中，现在它们又将直接进入厄尔尼诺带来的温暖水域。”一些物种，如岩鱼和鱿鱼，可能受益于较温暖的水域，“但总体而言，平衡更倾向于失败者，因为整个系统的生产力下降，”他说。“那里每个人的食物都减少了。”过去七年中每年都发生大规模海洋热浪，其中六次是自1982年开始记录以来东北太平洋最大的热浪之一。奥尼尔说，这些海洋热浪的增加与气候变化直接相关。“现在海洋热浪发生得更频繁，因为海洋在过去40年中持续变暖。”更多类似内容：• 在台风洪水中结婚的夫妇• 如何为100华氏度的城市降温？• 历史上最极端的飓风自20世纪70年代以来，海面温度显著加速上升，海洋吸收了气候变化中超过90%的多余热量。如今，海洋温度比以往任何时候都要高。邦德说，东北太平洋的热浪“正开始或多或少成为气候系统的永久特征”。莱辛指出，这是有记录以来第二次这种规模的海热浪与厄尔尼诺同时发生，并提到这两者之间的关系尚未完全理解。科学家仍在研究气候变化如何影响厄尔尼诺，但一致认为，由于全球变暖，本世纪这些事件的发生频率可能会增加。英国气象局的预测表明，随着厄尔尼诺达到顶峰，2026年晚些时候海面温度异常可能超过3摄氏度（5.4华氏度）。厄尔尼诺事件通常持续9至12个月，预计这次将在春季左右消散。海洋热浪将持续多久尚不清楚。“它们确实具有一些真正的持久性。‘斑点’有腿，”邦德说。只要太平洋水域仍然异常炎热，我们就可以预期天气和海洋生物会感受到影响。——要获取关键气候新闻和令人鼓舞的发展，请注册《未来地球》通讯，而《基本清单》每周两次提供精选的特写和见解。欲获取更多来自BBC的科学、技术、环境和健康故事，请在Facebook和Instagram上关注我们。地球气候极端天气洪水海洋环境"

readings.title: Is Italy the new tax haven for the global rich?
body: 22 April 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google John Laurenson Italy has already been attacked by the French Government for using tax incentives to lure wealthy French and other international residents away, but with the war in the Middle East hurting the Gulf states, Italy has become an even more attractive location for the rich. Tax wasn't the main reason for leaving France, Robert insists over a café crème at Charles de Gaulle airport. It was the beauty of Italy, the bella vita  (the beautiful/good life), the art and the music. But for the Frenchman, buying a house in Rome and becoming an Italian tax resident was a very nice part of the package offered by the country, where high net worth individuals can pay a fixed annual tax on all foreign income – regardless of amount – and enjoy a series of other exemptions.  Robert, who describes himself as only "moderately wealthy", moved to Italy eight years ago after a career in computers which ended with him selling his company. Robert, not his real name, may not be among the French billionaires who have fled the French taxman for Italy, but the advantages to him are clear.   If he'd been buying a house in France, he would have had to pay what the French call frais de notaire (solicitor's fees) most of which goes to the government (much like Stamp Duty in the UK or Real Estate Transfer Taxes in the US). In Italy there's an exemption for the prima casa , the first house you buy. In France, President Macron transformed France's Impot sur la Fortune  (wealth tax) into an Impot sur la Fortune Immobilière  (real estate wealth tax) so stock market investments, for example, are no longer affected but "if you have ten million dollars' worth of property, this tax is very painful indeed," says Robert. Again, there's nothing like that in Italy.  In France you also have to pay a property tax ( taxe foncière or land tax). "We don't have that here for the prima casa (first home)," says Robert, although he notes "there is a high charge for refuse collection". The best thing as far as he is concerned is that there is no inheritance tax on property you own in Italy up to €1 million ($1.1 million) and it's only 4% beyond that threshold. In France the tax-free limit is much lower – €100,000 ($110,000) – and beyond that it's a sliding scale up to a top rate of 45%. But it's for the seriously rich that Italy starts to look like a fiscal paradise. "I have friends who have moved here for tax reasons and others who are thinking about it," Robert tells me. "For people who really pay a lot of tax, Italy is very attractive because of it's "flat tax". In Italy, the taxman fixes an upper limit of tax that can be levied on income. However much you earn, you never pay more than that. The upper limit is now €300,000 ($353,000). Although not long ago it was €100,000 before rising to €200,000. If you're paying a million euros of income tax a year in France, Italy is very tempting. As for US citizens, Americans are always taxable on worldwide income, so moving to Italy would not help their tax bill. Even at €300,000, Italy's flat tax is still low for anyone making over €1m per year compared to anywhere else in Europe – Peter Ferrigno Robert tells me that he has two rich French friends who have moved to Italy in the past few months, but they came from the UK. They were both working in finance in the City of London and were keen to move to a place where the fiscal regime was as sympathetic to them as the one Britain had before it changed the rules for wealthy foreign residents.  "Even at €300,000, Italy's flat tax is still low for anyone making over €1m per year compared to anywhere else in Europe. And it means you get tax certainty and clarity, within the heart of Europe, rather than having to go a long way," says Peter Ferrigno, director of tax services at wealth migration specialists Henley & Partners. "We have meetings with people every week who would like to leave France," says Paris-based tax lawyer Jerome Barre. "They are unhappy about the tax situation now and they are worried that it will become harsher in the future. People are not confident with the political climate. Taxes are changing a lot, almost every year. People are frightened that after the election of the new president in 2027, things could become harder than today," he says. At this stage though it's more "questions from entrepreneurs and wealthy people who are wondering if they would like to move or not move rather than people actually moving," Jerome Barre explains. "Relocation requires full commitment and careful structuring," he stresses. He adds that for business-owners  " they need to change the seat of the company. They are subject in France to an exit tax." If many wealthy French people are at the "thinking-about-moving" stage, the question is being felt even more acutely in the United Arab Emirates. It's inevitable that many people will reconsider UAE – Peter Ferrigno But giving up on Dubai's zero-tax regime will be very difficult for many. "When you are in a country where you do not pay any tax, it's very difficult to come back to a country where you have to pay a lot. Especially for those used to spending a lot of money. The net in your pocket is very different, says Barre. And, he adds, people who have grown used to the zero-tax life "are not used to administrative formalities anymore – tax returns, documents – so it's not easy." More like this: • Dubai's tourism industry reels from 'brutal' impact of war • Why more Americans are now moving to Ireland • Is New York's cannabis business really flying high? "It's inevitable that many people will reconsider UAE," says Henley & Partners' Peter Ferrigno. "But I think it's far too early for people to wholesale uproot their life when it involves work, family, etc. The vast majority of people in the UAE are still regular people doing regular jobs, even most of the millionaires are millionaires because they are doing well paid jobs rather than being asset owners. If the war is relatively short, they will remain. If it drags on, then people will inevitably look elsewhere, or relocate the family and work remotely until it's safer. If you're in the UAE for work, there aren't likely to be that many equivalent roles in Italy," he says. However, it is likely that the war in the Middle East will dissuade many rich Europeans who would have otherwise moved there from re-locating to the UAE. Last year, Dubai was the number one destination by far for migrating millionaires, according to Henley & Partners. That number is bound to tumble in 2026, and with its attractive offer for the very wealthy, as well as its reputation for  la dolce vita  of course, it may well be Italy that benefits. -- For global insights and expert analysis for the boardroom and beyond, sign up to the  World of Business newsletter , while  The Essential List  delivers a handpicked selection of features and insights.  For more on business and beyond, follow us on  LinkedIn . 2026年4月22日 分享 保存 添加为Google首选 约翰·劳伦森 意大利已经遭到法国政府指责，称其利用税收优惠吸引富裕的法国人和其他国际居民迁居，但随着中东战争冲击海湾国家，意大利对富人而言变得更加具有吸引力。罗伯特在戴高乐机场喝着一杯咖啡奶油时坚称，税收并非他离开法国的主要原因，而是意大利的美景、美好生活、艺术和音乐。但对这位法国人来说，在罗马购房并成为意大利税务居民，是该国提供的一揽子方案中非常诱人的一部分，高净值个人可以对其所有外国收入缴纳固定年度税款——无论金额多少——并享受一系列其他豁免。 罗伯特自称只是“中等富裕”，在计算机行业打拼后卖掉了公司，八年前移居意大利。化名罗伯特的他不一定是那些逃离法国税务官员的法国亿万富翁之一，但对他而言好处显而易见。如果他在法国买房，他必须支付法国人所谓的公证费，其中大部分归政府所有（类似英国的印花税或美国的房产转让税）。在意大利，首次购房有豁免权。在法国，总统马克龙将法国的财富税转变为房地产财富税，因此股市投资等不再受影响，但“如果你拥有价值一千万美元的房产，这项税确实非常痛苦”，罗伯特说。而意大利没有类似税种。 在法国，你还必须缴纳房产税（土地税或地皮税）。罗伯特说：“我们这里对首套住房没有这种税”，不过他指出“垃圾收集费很高”。在他看来，最好的地方在于，在意大利拥有的房产价值不超过100万欧元（约110万美元）时，无需缴纳遗产税，超过该门槛仅需缴纳4%。而法国的免税限额低得多——10万欧元（约11万美元）——超过部分按累进税率最高达45%。但对超级富豪而言，意大利开始看起来像税收天堂。“我有朋友因税收原因搬到这里，还有人在考虑此事”，罗伯特告诉我。“对于真正缴纳高额税款的人来说，意大利非常吸引人，因为它实行‘固定税制’。在意大利，税务机构设定收入征税的上限。无论你赚多少，你支付的税额都不会超过这个上限。目前上限为30万欧元（约35.3万美元）。尽管

虽然不久之前这一数字还是10万欧元，后来涨到了20万欧元。如果你在法国每年缴纳100万欧元的所得税，意大利就非常有吸引力。至于美国公民，美国人总是要对全球收入征税，因此移居意大利对他们的税单没有帮助。即使是30万欧元，意大利的固定税对于年收入超过100万欧元的人来说，与欧洲其他任何地方相比仍然很低——彼得·费里尼奥·罗伯特告诉我，他有两位富有的法国朋友在过去几个月里搬到了意大利，但他们是从英国搬来的。他们两人都在伦敦金融城从事金融工作，渴望搬到一个税收制度对他们像英国在改变富裕外国居民规则之前那样有利的地方。

“即使是30万欧元，意大利的固定税对于年收入超过100万欧元的人来说，与欧洲其他任何地方相比仍然很低。而且这意味着你能在欧洲的心脏地带获得税收的确定性和清晰度，而不必远走他乡，”财富迁移专家恒理（Henley & Partners）税务服务总监彼得·费里尼奥说。“我们每周都会与想离开法国的人会面，”驻巴黎的税务律师杰罗姆·巴尔说。“他们对目前的税收状况感到不满，并担心未来会变得更加严苛。人们对政治气候缺乏信心。税收变化很大，几乎每年都在变。人们担心在2027年新总统当选后，情况会比今天更加艰难，”他说。不过，现阶段更多的是“企业家和富人在犹豫是否要搬走的问题，而不是真正在行动的人，”杰罗姆·巴尔解释道。“搬迁需要全身心投入和精心规划，”他强调。他补充说，对于企业主来说，“他们需要改变公司的注册地。他们在法国需要缴纳离境税。”

如果说许多法国富人正处于“考虑搬家”的阶段，那么这个问题在阿联酋则更为紧迫。彼得·费里尼奥表示，许多人不可避免地会重新考虑阿联酋。但对许多人来说，放弃迪拜的零税收制度将非常困难。“当你身处一个不缴税的国家，很难回到一个必须缴纳大量税款的国家。尤其是那些习惯了大手大脚花钱的人。你口袋里的净收入差别很大，”巴尔说。他还补充说，习惯了零税收生活的人“已经不再习惯行政手续——报税、文件——所以这并不容易。”更多类似内容：• 迪拜旅游业受战争‘残酷’影响而受挫 • 为什么更多美国人现在移居爱尔兰 • 纽约的大麻生意真的在蓬勃发展吗？

"不可避免的是，许多人会重新考虑阿联酋，"亨利合伙公司的彼得·费里尼奥表示。"但我认为，当涉及工作、家庭等问题时，现在说人们会大规模连根拔起还为时过早。阿联酋绝大多数人仍是从事普通工作的普通人，即使是大多数百万富翁，他们的财富也源于高薪工作，而非资产拥有。如果战争相对短暂，他们会留下；如果拖延下去，人们将不可避免地另寻他处，或搬迁家庭并远程工作，直到安全为止。如果你在阿联酋是为了工作，意大利恐怕不会有那么多同等职位，"他说。然而，中东战争很可能会劝阻许多原本会迁往阿联酋的富裕欧洲人。据亨利合伙公司数据，去年迪拜是百万富翁移民的首选目的地，遥遥领先。这一数字在2026年势必大幅下滑，而凭借对超级富豪的吸引力，以及其"甜蜜生活"的美誉，意大利很可能从中受益。——如需获取面向董事会及更广领域的全球洞察与专家分析，请订阅《商业世界》新闻简报，而《必备清单》则提供精选专题与见解。如需更多商业及更广泛内容，请在领英上关注我们。商业国际商业专题商业世界

readings.title: What would it take to actually stop the data centers?
body: Politics What would it take to actually stop the data centers? The AI buildout is bruised but still far from broken. by Eric Levitz Updated Sep 1, 2026, 2:45 PM UTC Gift Demonstrators wave signs during a nationwide protest against AI data center expansion in Imperial, California, on July 18, 2026. Sandy Huffaker/AFP via Getty Images Eric Levitz is a senior correspondent at Vox. He covers a wide range of political and policy issues with a special focus on questions that internally divide the American left and right. Before coming to Vox in 2024, he wrote a column on politics and economics for New York Magazine. In the United States, building a data center now polls roughly as well as abolishing the police . If current trends continue, server warehouses may soon be less popular with Americans than pizza topped with pineapple and shattered glass. In an August survey from Heatmap Pro and Embold Research, just 15 percent of Americans said they would support a data center being built in their area, while 75 percent expressed opposition. One year earlier, 43 percent of respondents in the same poll had approved of nearby data center development, while just 42 percent opposed it. Data center projects are increasingly unpopular and vulnerable to local opposition. Nevertheless, the AI infrastructure buildout remains massive. The economic forces driving the data center boom are extremely strong. Since AI data centers can be located almost anywhere, it’s difficult to stop them from being built somewhere . This soaring backlash is visible in other surveys — and in the actions of elected officials. In recent weeks, Wisconsin’s gubernatorial candidates sparred over who hates data centers more , Pennsylvania’s center-left Gov. Josh Shapiro enacted new restrictions on AI infrastructure projects (after previously championing such investment), and even Texas’s staunchly pro-business Republican government announced a temporary moratorium on new approvals. Meanwhile, data center projects are being canceled at a record rate , as local opposition mounts. This has led some in the pro-tech minority to worry that the data center buildout is about to collapse — and take the US economy down with it . Anti-AI commentators, for their part, are cheering the industry’s impending crisis . But such panic and celebration are both premature. In truth, despite exploding opposition, the data center boom is still going strong. Interviews with industry experts and recent construction data suggest that the economic forces driving the buildout remain more powerful than the political winds blowing against it. And unless Congress enacts a national moratorium, AI companies will almost certainly be able to continue finding jurisdictions willing to tolerate hyperscale campuses, in exchange for sufficient revenue and incentives. America’s data center boom can be slowed and geographically shifted. But it probably can’t be killed, absent a collapse in demand for computing power or a much bigger revolution in American politics. There are two fundamental facts about today’s data center boom: 1) The backlash against it is huge, and 2) the buildout is even bigger. The climate news outlet Heatmap has kept a tracker of new data center restrictions and cancellations. As of late July, it found that more than 500 jurisdictions had enacted severe constraints or bans on data center construction. The vast majority of these measures had been enacted since the beginning of this year. The publication also found that contested data center projects face a skyrocketing cancellation rate. In late 2024, 20 percent of disputed developments were canceled; in the first half of 2026, that figure was closer to 50 percent. By Heatmap’s tally, more than 100 data center projects have been nixed this year in the face of local opposition, while more than 200 are currently being fought. This surge of mass resistance is remarkable. And yet, it is also nowhere near sufficient to end the AI buildout. Although the number of places with severe restrictions (or outright bans) on server farms is rapidly rising, more than 90 percent of US counties had no significant constraints on data center development at July’s end. What’s more, many of the most eye-catching recent policy changes are less significant than they appear. For example, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott’s pause does not actually halt data center construction in the Lone Star State. Rather, it essentially establishes a more thorough screening process, when server farms apply for electricity from the state’s grid. Projects that supply all of their own power through on-site natural gas — as a rising share of new data centers do — are exempt. Pennsylvania and New York’s recently enacted restrictions on data center development are more substantial. Yet neither of those states are particularly important to the AI buildout. Taken together, New York and Pennsylvania host only about 6.5 percent of America’s data centers, according to Data Center Map . And their share of all pending developments is even more negligible, as the trade publication Construction Connect has illustrated : ConstructConnect Meanwhile, although half of contested data center projects are now failing, many still go undisputed. In the aggregate, cancellations have not kept pace with construction or new development. In the first quarter of this year, at least 3.5 gigawatts of data center capacity were canceled amid local opposition, in Heatmap’s tally. During the same three months, at least 36 GW of capacity were added to the US pipeline of proposed and active projects, according to the analytics firm Wood Mackenzie. As of April 1, that pipeline contained a total of 106 GW worth of developments that had already survived the permitting gauntlet. To be sure, cancellations have risen sharply since March. By Heatmap’s count, at least 13 gigawatts of capacity have been nixed so far this year. But the capacity of permitted projects has also grown since April 1. And the ratio between blocked and active developments has not radically changed, according to industry analysts. “At this point, we do not think the recent wave of opposition and policy intervention has materially changed our national capacity growth trajectory,” Maya Barkin, an analyst at the AI industry research firm SemiAnalysis , told me. Indeed, monthly construction spending on data centers in the US hit a record high this June. In short, data centers are marching forward despite taking heavy fire, like a pack of gut-shot zombies. Why has the AI buildout proven so resilient? There are at least two reasons. First, and most importantly, demand for computing power remains astronomical. As frontier AI companies have built out larger models — and consumers and companies have increased their use of artificial intelligence and digital services — our economy’s appetite for computation has far outstripped supply. According to a recent report from the commercial real estate firm JLL, 99 percent of North America’s data centers are occupied. What’s more, of the 66 GW of data center capacity currently being constructed in JLL’s count, 95 percent has already been reserved. Second, data center projects are unusually location-flexible. If a housing developer gets chased out of San Francisco’s suburbs by zoning rules and local opposition, it can’t relocate its condo tower to a mostly uninhabited stretch of Nevada desert . By contrast, data centers can — and do — operate in the middle of nowhere . For certain purposes, these facilities need some proximity to the users they serve; you can’t adequately support online gaming in New York City with data centers on the West Coast. But even in such cases, servers merely need to be in the same broad region. The hyperscale facilities used to train AI models, meanwhile, can be located virtually anywhere with land, fiber optic cables, a modicum of labor, and electricity (and now that many data centers are powering themselves through on-site natural gas plants, even the latter is potentially expendable). Taken together, these two realities make data center construction extremely difficult to choke off. Sky-high demand for compute means that hyperscalers can afford to throw a lot of money at localities, in order to secure a project’s approval. And location flexibility makes it very difficult for data center developers to run out of host jurisdictions, particularly when so many rural counties throughout the United States are starving for revenue and investment. Thus, unless Congress imposes a national moratorium, development deals will almost certainly keep getting struck. “I think companies will need to open up their wallets and make sure that communities receive clear benefits,” John Arnold, a billionaire investor and philanthropist who sits on Meta’s board (and whose foundation has given funding to Vox), told me. “There will be places that raise their hands and say, ‘For X amount of benefit, we will welcome you into the community.’” Just this week, West Virginia Gov. Patrick Morrisey signaled that he was moving forward with plans to encourage data center development and use the consequent revenue to slash the state’s income tax. On one level, all this may seem to validate anti-data center activism: If there are countless potential locations for these facilities, then why should any community host one it doesn’t want? This said, many oppose new data centers out of concern for their aggregate impacts, rather than their local ones. Climate activists fear that the AI buildout will generate perilous increases in carbon emissions. Populists on the right and left, meanwhile, want to slow the progress of artificial intelligence, so as to prevent the technology from causing mass unemployment — and/or human extinction . For these factions, the buildout’s resilience has more complicated implications. If state and local bans are unlikely to end the boom, then green groups might be unwise to push for such measures in relatively climate-conscious areas. After all, doing so could shift development toward jurisdictions with less renewable energy, and/or fewer restrictions on carbon pollution. Given that risk, blue-state environmentalists may do more to mitigate AI’s climate impacts by regulating data center development than by banning it. Specifically, climate groups could demand that hyperscalers help bankroll the vast expansions of clean energy and transmission infrastructure that the green transition has always required. For AI doomers, on the other hand, local bans may have some instrumental value. Moratoria and other restrictions are surely slowing the data center buildout at the margin. Still, as long as hyperscale facilities remain location-flexible — and tech companies stay well-capitalized — AI infrastructure will get built somewhere . A national moratorium could buy significant time. But ultimately, humanity’s security from the risks of AI hinges less on whether data centers get built than on what companies are allowed to do with them — and how the wealth they generate is distributed. The data center rebellion is among the most remarkable popular movements in recent memory. But it is arrayed against one of the largest investment frenzies in human history. Unless or until the AI industry’s alleged “ bubble ” bursts, its buildout will be exceptionally difficult to stop. Yet where that buildout happens, how it’s powered — and what communities extract from it — are all up for grabs (and, increasingly, being grabbed). ##段落
政治：究竟需要什么才能真的叫停数据中心？AI建设潮虽受挫，但远未破裂。作者：Eric Levitz，更新于2026年9月1日，下午2:45 UTC。礼品：2026年7月18日，加利福尼亚州因皮里尔，示威者在反对AI数据中心扩建的全国性抗议中挥舞标语。图片来源：Sandy Huffaker/AFP via Getty Images。Eric Levitz是Vox的高级记者，报道广泛的政治与政策议题，尤其关注美国左右翼内部分歧的问题。在2024年加入Vox之前，他为《纽约杂志》撰写政治与经济专栏。

##段落
在美国，如今建造数据中心的支持度，几乎与废除警察一样低。如果当前趋势持续，服务器仓库在美国人心中的受欢迎程度，可能很快就不如加了菠萝和碎玻璃的披萨。在Heatmap Pro和Embold Research于8月进行的一项调查中，仅15%的美国人表示支持在自家地区建造数据中心，而75%的人表示反对。一年前，同一民调中有43%的受访者赞成附近的数据中心开发，仅42%反对。数据中心项目越来越不受欢迎，也容易受到地方反对的冲击。

##段落
尽管如此，AI基础设施的建设规模依然庞大。推动数据中心繁荣的经济力量极为强劲。由于AI数据中心几乎可以建在任何地方，因此很难阻止它们在某处落地。这种日益高涨的反弹在其他调查中，以及民选官员的行动中都有体现。近几周，威斯康星州的州长候选人在谁更讨厌数据中心的问题上争执不休；宾夕法尼亚州中间派州长乔什·夏皮罗（此前曾大力支持此类投资）对AI基础设施项目实施了新限制；甚至一贯坚定亲商的得克萨斯州共和党政府也宣布暂停新项目审批。与此同时，随着地方反对声浪加剧，数据中心项目正以创纪录的速度被取消。

##段落
这导致科技界少数支持者担忧，数据中心建设潮可能即将崩溃，并将美国经济拖下水。反AI评论人士则对行业即将到来的危机欢呼雀跃。但这样的恐慌和庆祝都为时过早。事实上，尽管反对声激增，数据中心热潮依然强劲。对行业专家的采访和近期建设数据表明，推动建设的 economic 力量仍比反对它的政治风向更强大。除非国会颁布全国性暂停令，否则AI公司几乎肯定能继续找到愿意容忍超大规模园区、以换取充足回报的辖区。

充足的收入和激励。美国的数据中心建设热潮可以放缓，并在地理上转移，但除非计算能力需求崩溃或美国政治发生更大革命，否则它可能无法被扼杀。当今数据中心热潮有两个基本事实：1）对其的反弹巨大，2）建设规模甚至更大。气候新闻媒体Heatmap持续追踪新的数据中心限制和取消情况。截至7月底，它发现超过500个司法管辖区对数据中心建设实施了严格限制或禁令，其中绝大多数措施自今年年初以来已颁布。该媒体还发现，有争议的数据中心项目面临飙升的取消率。2024年底，20%的有争议开发项目被取消；2026年上半年，这一数字接近50%。根据Heatmap的统计，今年已有超过100个数据中心项目因地方反对而被取消，而200多个项目目前正在争议中。这种大规模抵抗的激增引人注目，但远不足以终结AI建设热潮。尽管对服务器农场实施严格限制（或完全禁止）的地方数量迅速增加，但截至7月底，美国超过90%的县对数据中心开发没有重大限制。此外，许多最引人注目的近期政策变化并不像表面看起来那么重要。例如，得克萨斯州州长格雷格·阿博特的暂停并未真正停止孤星州的数据中心建设，而是基本上建立了一个更彻底的筛选流程，当服务器农场向州电网申请电力时适用。通过现场天然气自行供应所有电力的项目——新数据中心中越来越多这样做的——则被豁免。宾夕法尼亚州和纽约州最近对数据中心开发的限制更为实质性，但这两个州对AI建设热潮并不特别重要。根据Data Center Map的数据，纽约和宾夕法尼亚合计仅占美国数据中心的约6.5%。而它们在所有待开发项目中的份额甚至更微不足道，正如行业出版物Construction Connect所示。与此同时，尽管一半的有争议数据中心项目现在失败，但许多项目仍未受争议。总体而言，取消并未跟上建设或新开发的步伐。根据Heatmap的统计，今年第一季度，至少有3.5吉瓦的数据中心容量因地方反对而被取消。在同一三个月内，至少有36吉瓦的容量被添加到美国的拟议和活跃项目管线中。

根据分析公司伍德麦肯齐的数据，截至4月1日，该管道中总计包含106吉瓦的已通过许可审核的开发项目。诚然，自3月以来，取消数量急剧上升。根据Heatmap的统计，今年迄今至少有13吉瓦的容量被取消。但自4月1日以来，已获许可项目的容量也有所增长。据行业分析师称，受阻项目与活跃项目之间的比例并未发生根本性变化。“目前，我们认为最近的反对浪潮和政策干预并未实质性地改变我们的全国容量增长轨迹，”AI行业研究公司SemiAnalysis的分析师Maya Barkin告诉我。事实上，美国数据中心月度建设支出在今年6月创下历史新高。简而言之，数据中心尽管遭受重创，仍在向前推进，就像一群腹部中弹的僵尸。为什么AI建设如此具有韧性？至少有两个原因。首先，也是最重要的，对计算能力的需求仍然巨大。随着前沿AI公司构建更大规模的模型——以及消费者和企业增加对人工智能和数字服务的使用——我们经济对计算的需求已远远超过供应。根据商业房地产公司仲量联行最近的一份报告，北美99%的数据中心已被占用。此外，在仲量联行统计的目前正在建设的66吉瓦数据中心容量中，95%已被预订。其次，数据中心项目在选址上具有异常灵活性。如果住宅开发商因分区法规和当地反对而被赶出旧金山郊区，它无法将其公寓大楼迁移到内华达沙漠中大部分无人居住的地带。相比之下，数据中心可以——而且确实——在偏远地区运营。对于某些用途，这些设施需要靠近它们服务的用户；你不能仅靠西海岸的数据中心来充分支持纽约市的在线游戏。但即使在这些情况下，服务器也只需位于同一大区域即可。用于训练AI模型的超大规模设施，则几乎可以位于任何拥有土地、光纤电缆、少量劳动力和电力的地方（而且现在许多数据中心通过现场天然气发电厂自供电，甚至后者也可能变得不必要）。综合来看，这两个现实使得数据中心建设极难被扼杀。对计算的高需求意味着超大规模企业能够向地方投入大量资金以确保项目获批。而选址灵活性使数据中心开发商很难找不到落户地。

鉴于美国众多农村县镇正亟需财政收入与投资，这些司法管辖区的抵制尤其可能松动。因此，除非国会实施全国性暂停令，开发协议几乎肯定会继续达成。“我认为企业需要打开钱包，确保社区获得明确利益，”Meta董事会成员、亿万富翁投资者兼慈善家约翰·阿诺德（其基金会曾资助Vox）告诉我，“会有地方举手说，‘只要带来X数额的好处，我们就欢迎你入驻社区。’”就在本周，西弗吉尼亚州州长帕特里克·莫里西表示，他正推进鼓励数据中心开发并利用由此产生的收入大幅削减州所得税的计划。从某种层面看，这一切似乎印证了反数据中心行动主义的合理性：如果这些设施有无数潜在选址，那为何任何社区要接纳一个自己不想要的？尽管如此，许多人反对新建数据中心是出于对其总体影响的担忧，而非本地影响。气候活动家担心AI建设热潮会导致碳排放危险地增加。与此同时，左右翼民粹主义者希望减缓人工智能的发展，以防止该技术造成大规模失业——和/或人类灭绝。对这些派别而言，建设热潮的韧性具有更复杂的含义。如果州和地方禁令不太可能终结这一繁荣，那么环保团体在相对气候意识较强的地区推动此类措施可能并不明智。毕竟，这样做可能将开发转向可再生能源较少、碳污染限制较少的司法管辖区。鉴于这一风险，蓝州环保主义者可能通过监管数据中心开发而非禁止来更好地缓解AI的气候影响。具体而言，气候团体可以要求超大规模运营商帮助资助绿色转型一直所需的清洁能源和输电基础设施的大规模扩展。另一方面，对于AI末日论者来说，地方禁令可能具有一些工具性价值。暂停令和其他限制措施肯定在边际上减缓了数据中心建设。然而，只要超大规模设施选址灵活——且科技公司资本充足——AI基础设施总会在某处建成。全国性暂停令可能争取到宝贵时间。但归根结底，人类免受AI风险的安全保障，与其说取决于数据中心是否建成，不如说取决于企业被允许用它们做什么——以及所创造的财富如何分配。数据中心反抗运动是近年最引人注目的民众运动之一。但它只是……

##段落
这是人类历史上最大规模的投资狂潮之一。除非AI行业所谓的“泡沫”破裂，否则其建设将极难阻止。然而，建设发生在何处、如何为其提供动力——以及社区从中获得什么——都尚待争夺（且正日益被争夺）。查看更多：人工智能 创新 政治 技术

readings.title: How social media ceased to be social
body: 22 May 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google John Laurenson Social media platforms used to be about communication between friends – now many are increasingly short video entertainment hubs. The business model is to increase the time people spend on their apps and increase ad revenue. But is there already a consumer backlash? Aurélia fixes herself a coffee, sits down in her beautiful garden not far from Paris and goes on Instagram "to relax." First up: "a guy I like a lot who does interior design. He's in Venice at the moment." She's into interior design, and has even just had two bird drawings by the 19th Century English designer William Morris tattooed on her arms. She scrolls down. Two kittens having a fight. "I love animals so I get a lot of animals. That's how it works, social media. You click on bananas and they give you bananas." There are ads too – although they look just like the other posts – for a robot-vacuum cleaner, a diet and bed linen (with Morris-inspired designs). But no friends. She has 198 on Instagram but she says "it's completely changed. I practically don’t see any friends' posts anymore." She’s pretty much given up posting herself. "I don't think anyone sees them anymore anyway."  While there remain committed social, amateur posters on Instagram and especially Facebook, the switch from communicating with people you know to scrolling through professionally made content from people you don't, is even more pronounced among young users. Kylian, 16, is in vocational training to become a chef. He's on TikTok and Youtube a lot, he says. "I like looking at videos more than photos or messages. I watch videos made by people I don't know. I don’t post at all. I'm a rather shy person. I stay in my bubble. I watch and that’s all. I keep my reactions to myself." "I spend a lot of time scrolling through videos made by content-creators," says Lucie, also 16. "They're more interesting than the posts of people I know." She doesn't post except sometimes "stories" which disappear after 24 hours.  Whether it's TikTok, Snapchat, Facebook and Instagram, we are a long way from the "digital town square" of personal interaction that social media was even just a few years ago. In France, annual official Barometre du numerique 2026  shows 49% of social media users are "active only occasionally". In the UK, an Ofcom report   published in April showed a year-on-year drop of users who actively post from 61% to 49%. In the US, a Morning Consult survey of June last year found 28% reported posting less often than the previous year. Just 33% now post daily compared to 57% who use it for entertainment daily. The gap is a lot wider still for Gen Z – 18% active for 74% passive. Vanessa Lalo, a Paris-based clinical psychologist specialising in on-line behaviour, says "users have become more conscious that the traces you leave (on social media) stay there forever and some no longer want to maintain social media relations that can be superficial. Some don’t want the exposure to criticism that might be a risk when you post or the feeling that their post will seem poor alongside all the professional content". However, Lalo adds, people haven’t stopped posting, rather they are posting different things and in different places. "On TikTok, for example, young people publish a lot of content but it's more funny parodies and remixes of existing material. The goal is to make people laugh, not to tell people about their lives." That still happens, she says, but it’s moved from social media platforms like Instagram and Facebook to messaging sites like WhatsApp. There's also been a move towards private groups on Instagram and Snapchat. "These are much more intimate places where you're not bombarded with ads and content made by influencers," she says. "What we're seeing is social media splitting in two," says social media consultant Matt Navarra, author of the Geekout Newsletter. "Big platforms like Instagram and TikTok are becoming more about entertainment and discovery. WhatsApp is becoming the place people go to actually be social. The catch is, those kinds of spaces are harder for companies to make money from." Small business owners are being pushed to become presenters, editors, trend spotters and content creators, on top of actually running the business – Matt Navarra It was TikTok that helped to pioneer an algorithm that figures out from the moment you start scrolling what you like, and then fills your feed with material calculated to keep you on the app for the longest possible time. Now, says Matt Navarra, "Meta has built what it calls an AI system for unconnected content recommendations on Facebook and Instagram, which basically means, they're increasingly showing you stuff from people you don't follow because the machine thinks you're going to like it. It's not biased towards, is it a professional creator? Is it a brand? Is it a friend? If they can see that you've engaged with a friend a lot, you might see a lot more of their content. It's just that who you are friends with, who you follow, has become irrelevant in a way." This all means that small businesses, that have long used social media for free promotion have to up their game.   "There's a real opportunity for some small businesses," says Matt Navarra. "A bakery, florist, salon or local café can still break through if they have a good story, strong visuals or behind-the-scenes content people want to watch. But it also means the job has changed. Small business owners are being pushed to become presenters, editors, trend spotters and content creators, on top of actually running the business." The social platforms continue to be monetised predominantly by ad revenue. That is still the core business model. And ad revenue continues to grow – Matt Navarra Social media is evolving into something passive like television, albeit television that adapts as you zap. Or rather which knows you so well that it doesn't seem to matter that much that it's taken the remote control. You give the platform information about yourself that it uses for commercial gain and, in return, it gives you content tailored to please you for free. The transition from truly social media to entertainment platform does seem to be paying off. "The social platforms continue to be monetised predominantly by ad revenue. That is still the core business model. And ad revenue continues to grow," says Matt Navarra. Global social media ad revenue is expected to reach $317 billion (£236bn) in 2026, up from $277 billion (£206bn) last year. Meta is the biggest winner. Its ad sales already increased 22% year-on-year in 2025.  Ad sales are expected to hit $243 billion (£181bn) this year , enough to overtake Google for the first time. AI powered digital ad targeting is becoming ever more effective and precise. "The social platforms allow companies to put ads amongst the content that you're scrolling through. Every third or fourth scroll is an ad. And they are the world's best ad targeting engines. They know so much about your interests because of what you've looked at, liked, engaged with, what you've chosen to follow, the time you've spent in certain areas of the app, things like that," Navarra says.  "So advertisers will go in and say: 'I want to place an ad next to people in the UK who are between thirty and sixty years old and who are interested in DIY' and the social platforms will have that information and will place the ads accordingly." The price will depend on the number of impressions (clicks) the advertiser wants and how tight the criteria are. It costs more to place ads in the social media feeds of people who buy horses than people who buy ice-cream. More like this: •  TikTok is tracking you, even if you don't use the app. Here's how to stop it •  How to stop AI from turning your brain to mush •  This monkey selfie will protect you from AI slop Might there be a backlash coming? Don't many people go on to social media to see how friends are reacting to their posts or comments before settling down to scroll through professionally made content? Whether it's the shrinking social motivation to get on these apps or something else, the amount of time people spend on social media plateaued at an average of 141 minutes in 2025, down slightly from 143 minutes in 2024 . However, this is only part of the story, as the number of people using social media and the total time humanity spends on these apps continues to rise. For Gen Z it’s higher still. Around five hours a day in the United States where, for this demographic, social media has also become the primary search engine and shopping tool. Meanwhile, for those who miss what are fast becoming the old days when social media enabled you to share a bit of your life, a joke or a point of view with people you more-or-less knew, there are tools within platforms, says Matt Navarra, that allow you to choose to see mainly friends and family content. "People can flick to a feed that gives them that," he says. "But most people don't." -- If you liked this story, sign up for The Essential List newsletter – a handpicked selection of features, videos and can't-miss news, delivered to your inbox twice a week.   For more on business and beyond, follow us on  LinkedIn . 2026年5月22日 分享 保存 设为Google偏好 John Laurenson 社交媒体平台曾经是朋友之间交流的工具——如今，许多平台正日益成为短视频娱乐中心。其商业模式是增加人们在应用上花费的时间，并提升广告收入。但消费者是否已经开始产生抵触情绪？ Aurélia给自己泡了杯咖啡，坐在巴黎附近美丽的花园里，上Instagram“放松一下”。首先映入眼帘的是：“一个我非常喜欢的家伙，他做室内设计。他现在在威尼斯。”她热衷室内设计，甚至刚刚把19世纪英国设计师威廉·莫里斯的两幅鸟类画作纹在手臂上。她向下滑动屏幕。两只小猫在打架。“我热爱动物，所以看到很多动物内容。社交媒体就是这样运作的。你点击香蕉，他们就给你看香蕉。”还有广告——尽管它们看起来和其他帖子一样——涉及扫地机器人、减肥餐和床单（带有莫里斯风格设计）。但没有朋友的内容。她在Instagram上有198个粉丝，但她说“情况完全变了。我几乎再也看不到任何朋友的帖子了。”她自己也基本放弃了发帖。“我觉得反正也没人看了。” 尽管在Instagram，尤其是Facebook上，仍有一些忠实的社交型业余发帖者，但从与认识的人交流转向浏览陌生人制作的专业内容，这一趋势在年轻用户中尤为显著。16岁的Kylian正在接受厨师职业培训。他说自己经常刷TikTok和YouTube。“我喜欢看视频，胜过看照片或消息。我看的是不认识的人制作的视频。我完全不发帖。我是个比较害羞的人。我待在自己的小圈子里。我只看，仅此而已。我把自己的反应藏在心里。” “我花很多时间刷内容创作者制作的视频，”同为16岁的Lucie说。“它们比认识的人的帖子更有趣。”她除了偶尔发些24小时后消失的“快拍”外，并不发帖。 无论是TikTok、Snapchat、Facebook还是Instagram，我们早已远离了社交媒体几年前那种个人互动的“数字城镇广场”。在法国，2026年官方年度《数字晴雨表》显示，49%的社交媒体用户“仅偶尔活跃”。在英国，4月发布的Ofcom报告显示，积极发帖的用户同比下降，从61%降至49%。在美国，去年6月Morning Consult的一项调查发现，28%的人表示发帖频率低于前一年。如今只有33%的人每天发帖，而57%的人每天将其用于娱乐。对于Z世代来说，这一差距更大——18%为活跃用户，74%为被动用户。巴黎临床心理学家Vanessa Lalo专注于在线行为研究，她表示...

她说：“用户已经意识到，（在社交媒体上）留下的痕迹会永远存在，一些人不再想维持那些可能肤浅的社交媒体关系。有些人不想暴露在发帖可能带来的批评风险中，或者担心自己的帖子在众多专业内容旁显得逊色。”然而，拉洛补充道，人们并没有停止发帖，而是发布的内容和地点发生了变化。“例如，在TikTok上，年轻人发布大量内容，但更多是对现有素材的有趣模仿和混剪。目标是逗人发笑，而不是讲述自己的生活。”她说，这种分享生活的内容依然存在，但已从Instagram和Facebook等社交媒体平台转移到了WhatsApp等即时通讯网站。此外，还出现了转向Instagram和Snapchat私人群组的趋势。“这些是更私密的空间，你不会被广告和网红内容轰炸，”她说。

“我们看到的是社交媒体正在一分为二，”社交媒体顾问、《极客通讯》作者马特·纳瓦拉说。“Instagram和TikTok等大型平台正更多地转向娱乐和发现功能。WhatsApp则成为人们真正进行社交的地方。问题在于，这类空间对企业来说更难盈利。”

正是TikTok率先开创了一种算法，能从你开始滑动的那一刻起判断出你的喜好，然后填满你的信息流，用计算好的内容让你尽可能长时间留在应用上。现在，马特·纳瓦拉表示，“Meta已在Facebook和Instagram上建立了一个所谓的人工智能系统，用于推荐非关联内容，这基本上意味着，它们越来越多地向你展示你不关注的人的内容，因为机器认为你会喜欢。它不会偏向于判断内容是否来自专业创作者、品牌还是朋友。如果它发现你和某个朋友互动频繁，你可能会看到更多他们的内容。只是，你的朋友是谁、你关注了谁，在某种程度上已变得无关紧要。”这一切意味着，长期以来利用社交媒体免费推广的小企业必须提升自己的水平。

“一些小企业确实有机会，”马特·纳瓦拉说。“面包店、花店、沙龙或本地咖啡馆，只要有好故事、吸引人的视觉效果或人们想看的幕后内容，仍然可以突围。但这也意味着工作方式已经改变。小企业主正被迫在经营业务之外，同时成为主持人、编辑、潮流观察者和内容创作者。”

实际经营业务的层面。”社交媒体平台依然主要通过广告收入实现商业化，这仍是其核心商业模式，且广告收入持续增长——马特·纳瓦拉指出。社交媒体正演变为类似电视的被动媒介，尽管这种电视会随你切换而调整，或者说它对你了解之深，以至于即便它拿走了遥控器，似乎也无伤大雅。你向平台提供关于自身的信息，平台借此牟利，作为回报，它免费为你推送量身定制、取悦你的内容。从真正意义上的社交媒体向娱乐平台的转型似乎正在奏效。“社交媒体平台依然主要通过广告收入实现商业化，这仍是其核心商业模式，且广告收入持续增长，”马特·纳瓦拉表示。全球社交媒体广告收入预计将从去年的2770亿美元（2060亿英镑）增至2026年的3170亿美元（2360亿英镑）。Meta是最大赢家，其2025年广告销售额已同比增长22%，预计今年将达到2430亿美元（1810亿英镑），首次超越谷歌。AI驱动的数字广告定向投放正变得愈发高效精准。“社交媒体平台允许企业在你浏览的内容中插入广告，每滚动三四次就会看到一条广告。它们是全球最优秀的广告定向引擎，通过你查看、点赞、互动的内容、关注的账号以及在应用内特定区域停留的时间等，对你的兴趣了如指掌，”纳瓦拉说。“因此广告主会提出要求：‘我想向英国30至60岁、对DIY感兴趣的人群投放广告’，平台掌握这些信息，便会精准投放。”广告价格取决于广告主所需的曝光量（点击次数）以及目标条件的精确程度。在购买马匹的人群的社交媒体信息流中投放广告，成本高于购买冰淇淋的人群。更多相关内容：• TikTok在追踪你，即使你不用该应用——如何阻止它 • 如何防止AI把你的大脑变成浆糊 • 这张猴子自拍照将保护你免受AI垃圾内容侵害。是否会迎来反弹？难道许多人上社交媒体不是为了先看看朋友对自己帖子和评论的反应，然后才沉下心来浏览专业制作的内容吗？无论是使用这些应用的社交动机减弱还是其他原因，2025年人们在社交媒体上花费的时间平均为141分钟，与2024年的143分钟相比略有下降，呈现平稳态势。然而，这只是故事的一部分，因为使用社交媒体的人数仍在增长。

全球范围内，人类在这些应用上花费的总时间持续攀升。对于Z世代而言，这一数字更高，在美国，他们每天大约花费五小时，社交媒体已成为这一群体的主要搜索引擎和购物工具。与此同时，对于那些怀念社交媒体曾让你能与熟人分享生活片段、笑话或观点的“昔日时光”的人，平台内提供了工具，马特·纳瓦拉指出，允许你选择主要查看朋友和家人的内容。“人们可以切换到那样的信息流，”他说，“但大多数人不会这么做。”——如果你喜欢这个故事，请订阅《必备清单》新闻通讯，这是一份精选的特色、视频和不容错过的新闻，每周两次发送到你的邮箱。欲了解更多商业及其他领域内容，请在LinkedIn上关注我们。商业科技特写社交媒体商业世界。

readings.title: The bears cooling off in a California pool
body: 4 days ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Isabelle Gerretsen Black bears love lounging in Brian Gordon and Ricardo Martinez's pool in Los Angeles. As bear encounters increase across Southern California, the couple share videos of their furry visitors and reveal how they are co-existing with these wild animals. When Brian Gordon first learned that black bears were swimming in the pool of the house he was buying in Los Angeles, he was very afraid. "I'd never seen a bear in real life. I said, 'We'll just build a big wall with barbed wire,'" he recalls. Four years later, Gordon loves nothing more than seeing a family of bears playing in his pool and running around his garden. The furry visitors stop by several times a week. (Scroll down to watch a video of the bears at play.) "They are fine to come here and scratch on the trees, take a nap, and jump in the pool if it's hot, as long as we're not creating harm for them, or for ourselves," Gordon says. Gordon and his partner Ricardo Martinez have made it their mission to peacefully share their pool and garden with the bears. But behind these charming videos of bears relaxing in their pool, there's a deeper story of vigilance and safety precautions that make this co-existence possible. The couple live in Monrovia, Los Angeles County, in Southern California, home to around 1,600 bears . Their house is in the foothills of the San Gabriel Mountains and borders the Angeles National Forest, which spans 700,000 acres (2,830sq km). When the couple moved in, they started spotting bears almost immediately. They initially tried to chase the bears away by yelling, using air horns and occasionally a paintball gun with soft rubber pellets. "But it felt horrible," says Martinez. "It did not sit right with us. We said that as long as they're not breaking into the home and getting into the trash, then they're ok to come by." They sought an approach that would keep both themselves and the bears safe, despite close proximity. "We've since settled on less aggressive means, and honestly, they work better for us," says Gordon. We have had bears crashing barbecues – Brian Gordon Martinez says that black bears are "misunderstood". "They are not going to eat you," says Martinez. Black bear attacks are incredibly rare, with just one fatal attack recorded in California's history .  The couple say they always keep a "healthy distance" from the bears and stay inside when the animals are around. There are sometimes unplanned encounters though.  "We have had bears crashing barbecues," says Gordon. "But if they see you, they usually just walk away." Gordon and Martinez say their favourite bear visitor is Maddie, who they first got to know as an incredibly inquisitive youngster in 2023. She loved playing in the pool and hanging around the garden. "She is our golden child," says Martinez. A year later, Maddie returned with her cubs in tow. "Unfortunately she lost those cubs, so we went through an emotional rollercoaster with her," says Martinez. This year she has brought her new cubs to the house. "They're the most adorable [creatures] you've ever seen. They're so cuddly but also intimidating, with their long claws." We live here and the bears live here. We don't want them to go anywhere – Ricardo Martinez Punky is another "rambunctious yearling" who first came to the house as a cub with her mother, says Gordon. "She would pop all the pool floaties." She once climbed onto an inflatable cupcake and drifted into the middle of the pool. "She really stole our hearts that summer with her pool fun," says Gordon. They nicknamed another regular visitor "Nappy", as the female bear likes to take long siestas while floating in the pool. "She'll literally go to the steps of the pool, get in and put her head down. She's the only bear I've seen take hour-long naps in the pool," says Gordon. If she sees the couple, Nappy will huff at them. "She's a big mama bear and she's just a little grumpy about everything in life," Gordon jokes. These characters are among a growing number of black bears trying to make a home alongside Californians , and often posing challenges for local communities.  There are more than 60,000 black bears living in California , says Wilson Sherman, a research fellow at the University of California, Los Angeles. The wild animals are an increasingly common sight in LA suburbs. "They are really intelligent, adaptable omnivores. They eat everything and have learned how to gain calories in places where people live," says Sherman, who studies how communities respond to black bears.  Not all bear encounters are as positive as Gordon and Martinez's experience though. "We do see incidents pretty regularly of bears raiding trash and entering homes," says Sherman. "The really sad thing about this is that when things go awry, it's usually the bears that end up paying the price. Several bears have been put down in the last few years."   A mother black bear called Blondie was euthanised by the California Department of Fish and Wildlife in March 2026 after she swiped at a woman walking her dog in Monrovia.  Blondie had also visited Gordon and Martinez's garden a few times and never caused any problems. Gordon organised a petition to try to prevent the euthanasia, which was signed by almost 6,000 people. "It was pretty devastating. Blondie resembles all mama bears, just trying to find shelter, to raise her kids and live her life," he says. The California Department of Fish and Wildlife says that DNA testing revealed that the captured bear was responsible for the incident, as well as a previous attack on an elderly resident sitting on his porch in Monrovia in June 2025. "Euthanasia is used only as a last resort when an animal poses a risk to public safety and cannot be safely returned to the wild," says a spokesperson. "Relocation may seem like a solution but is not an option when it could put public safety at risk. Bears have strong spatial memory and often return to familiar areas." The bear's cubs are being cared for at a wildlife rehabilitation centre and will be released into a suitable habitat when they are ready, he adds. To minimise conflict with bears, Sherman says it is important that communities restrict access to attractants, such as rubbish bins and leaving food outdoors.  "For a bear, finding a box that's full of pizza when you've been spending your time digging for worms and roots is a game changer." Keeping neighbourhoods bear-free is a "collective training effort", Sherman adds. "You all have to be on the same page, because if one person's leaving a lot of really good stuff in their yard, the bear is very likely going to think, 'I should check out a handful of other yards.'" Gordon says that they are "hypervigilant" when it comes to waste. "We don't even use our trash cans. I haul it to my office, a couple of times a week." They also keep their doors and windows closed and don't ever leave food in their car. They're not teddy bears, they are still wild animals – Wilson Sherman The couple say they have never had a negative encounter with any of the bears visiting their home. Martinez once found Nappy in the garage when he'd accidentally left it open. "We both startled each other," he says. "I slowly walked back, because you don't ever want to corner a bear." She emerged from the garage and went on her way, he says. More like this:
Why grizzly bears need their own hiking trails
The true story of Germany ' s rampant raccoons

Social media accounts, like Martinez and Gordon's, and home surveillance cameras are allowing people "to understand bears as individuals and providing an intimate look into their lives", says Sherman. But he has some reservations. "There's always the risk of Disneyfication, of painting too fuzzy a picture. They're not teddy bears, they are still wild animals." Sherman warns that it is important that bears and humans don't become too comfortable around each other. "Part of loving bears is creating healthy boundaries and setting the bears up for success when they inevitably pass through our neighbourhoods," he says. Through their Instagram account, @poolbearlife, Gordon and Martinez hope to raise awareness of how people can behave safely around bears and how to mitigate unwanted encounters. They stress that their relationship with black bears is not something that could necessarily be universal. "This works for us, for where we live," says Gordon.  "It's all about finding that balance with wildlife, how can we co-thrive?" says Martinez. "We live here and the bears live here. We don't want them to go anywhere." -- For essential climate news and hopeful developments to your inbox, sign up to the  Future Earth newsletter, while  The Essential List delivers a handpicked selection of features and insights twice a week.   For more science, technology, environment and health stories from the BBC, follow us on  Facebook and  Instagram . ##段落
4天前 分享 保存 设为Google首选 伊莎贝尔·格雷森 黑熊喜欢在布莱恩·戈登和里卡多·马丁内斯位于洛杉矶的泳池里消遣。随着南加州熊类目击事件日益增多，这对夫妇分享了毛茸茸访客的视频，并揭示了他们如何与这些野生动物共存。当布莱恩·戈登第一次得知黑熊正在他打算购买的洛杉矶房子的泳池里游泳时，他非常害怕。“我这辈子从没见过熊。我说，‘我们就建一堵带铁丝网的大墙吧，’”他回忆道。四年后，戈登最喜欢的莫过于看到一家熊在他的泳池里玩耍、在他的花园里跑来跑去。这些毛茸茸的访客每周都会光顾好几次。（向下滚动观看熊玩耍的视频。）“它们来这里抓抓树、打个盹、热了就跳进泳池，这都没问题，只要我们不伤害它们，它们也不伤害我们就行，”戈登说。戈登和他的伴侣里卡多·马丁内斯把与熊和平共享泳池和花园视为自己的使命。但在这些熊在泳池里放松的迷人视频背后，有一个关于警惕和安全防范的更深层故事，正是这些努力让这种共存成为可能。这对夫妇住在南加州洛杉矶县的蒙罗维亚，那里大约有1600只熊。他们的房子位于圣盖博山脉的山麓，紧邻占地70万英亩（2830平方公里）的安吉利斯国家森林。这对夫妇搬进来后，几乎立刻就开始看到熊出没。他们最初试图通过大喊大叫、使用气喇叭，偶尔用装软橡胶弹丸的彩弹枪来驱赶熊。“但那感觉很糟糕，”马丁内斯说。“我们心里过意不去。我们说，只要它们不闯进屋里、不翻垃圾桶，那它们来转转就没问题。”他们寻求一种既能保护自己又能保护熊安全的方法，尽管彼此距离很近。“我们后来采用了不那么激进的手段，说实话，对我们来说效果更好，”戈登说。

##段落
我们遇到过熊闯入烧烤派对的情况——布莱恩·戈登 马丁内斯说，黑熊“被误解了”。“它们不会吃你的，”马丁内斯说。黑熊袭击事件极为罕见，加州历史上仅记录过一起致命袭击。这对夫妇表示，他们总是与熊保持“安全距离”，当动物在附近时就会待在室内。不过偶尔也会有意外相遇。“我们遇到过熊闯入烧烤派对的情况，”戈登说。“但如果它们看到你，通常只会走开。”戈登和马丁内斯说，他们最喜欢的熊访客是Maddie，他们第一次认识她是在2023年，当时她还是个极其好奇的小家伙。她喜欢在泳池里玩耍，喜欢在周围闲逛。

##段落
还有花园。“她是我们的金童，”马丁内斯说。一年后，麦迪带着她的幼崽回来了。“不幸的是，她失去了那些幼崽，所以我们和她一起经历了情绪上的过山车，”马丁内斯说。今年，她带着新的幼崽来到了房子。“它们是你见过的最可爱的[生物]。它们非常惹人喜爱，但也令人敬畏，因为它们有长长的爪子。”我们住在这里，熊也住在这里。我们不想让它们去任何地方——里卡多·马丁内斯

##段落
Punky是另一只“精力充沛的一岁熊”，戈登说，她第一次作为幼崽和母亲一起来到房子。“她会把所有泳池浮具都弄破。”有一次，她爬上一个充气纸杯蛋糕，漂到了泳池中央。“那个夏天，她在泳池里的玩耍真的俘获了我们的心，”戈登说。他们给另一位常客起了个绰号叫“纳皮”，因为这头母熊喜欢在泳池里漂浮时打长盹。“她真的会走到泳池台阶边，进去，然后低下头。她是我见过的唯一一头会在泳池里睡上一个小时午觉的熊，”戈登说。如果纳皮看到这对夫妇，她会朝他们喷气。“她是个熊妈妈，对生活中一切都有点脾气暴躁，”戈登开玩笑说。

##段落
这些角色是越来越多试图与加州人共同安家的黑熊中的一部分，它们常常给当地社区带来挑战。加州大学洛杉矶分校研究员威尔逊·谢尔曼说，加州生活着超过6万只黑熊。这些野生动物在洛杉矶郊区越来越常见。“它们是非常聪明、适应性强的杂食动物。它们什么都吃，并且学会了如何在人类居住的地方获取卡路里，”研究社区如何应对黑熊的谢尔曼说。

##段落
不过，并非所有与熊的相遇都像戈登和马丁内斯的经历那样积极。“我们确实经常看到熊翻垃圾、闯入民宅的事件，”谢尔曼说。“真正可悲的是，当事情出错时，通常是熊最终付出代价。过去几年里，有几只熊被处死。”

##段落
一只名叫布隆迪的母黑熊于2026年3月被加州鱼类和野生动物部门实施安乐死，此前她在蒙罗维亚袭击了一名遛狗的女性。布隆迪也曾几次造访戈登和马丁内斯的花园，从未造成任何问题。戈登组织了一份请愿书，试图阻止安乐死，近6000人签署了这份请愿书。“这非常令人痛心。布隆迪像所有熊妈妈一样，只是想寻找庇护所，抚养孩子并过自己的生活，”他说。加州鱼类和野生动物部门表示，DNA检测显示，被捕获的这头熊对事件负有责任，也应对先前的一起事件负责。

此前在2025年6月，蒙罗维亚一名老年居民坐在自家门廊时曾遭到袭击。“安乐死仅作为最后手段，在动物对公共安全构成威胁且无法安全放归野外时使用，”一位发言人表示。“重新安置看似可行，但当其可能危及公共安全时便非选项。熊具有强大的空间记忆，常常会返回熟悉区域。”他补充说，这只熊的幼崽正在一家野生动物康复中心接受照料，待时机成熟后将放归适宜栖息地。谢尔曼指出，为尽量减少与熊的冲突，社区必须限制接触诱因，如垃圾箱和户外遗留食物。“对一只熊来说，当你一直挖虫子吃树根时，发现一个装满披萨的盒子简直是改变人生的大事。”他补充道，保持社区无熊是一项“集体训练努力”。“你们必须步调一致，因为如果某个人院子里留了大量好东西，熊很可能想，‘我应该去检查其他几个院子。’”戈登表示，他们在垃圾处理方面“高度警惕”。“我们甚至不用自家垃圾桶。我每周几次把它拖到办公室。”他们还保持门窗紧闭，从不在车内留食物。它们不是泰迪熊，仍是野生动物——威尔逊·谢尔曼。这对夫妇表示，他们从未与到访家中的熊有过负面接触。马丁内斯有次不小心让车库门开着，发现纳皮在内。“我们互相吓了一跳，”他说，“我慢慢后退，因为你绝不想困住一只熊。”他称，它走出车库便离开了。更多类似内容：为什么灰熊需要自己的远足小径；看到熊时该怎么办；德国浣熊泛滥的真实故事。谢尔曼表示，像马丁内斯和戈登这样的社交媒体账号及家庭监控摄像头，使人们能够“理解熊作为个体的特性，并深入了解它们的生活”。但他也有所保留。“总有迪士尼化的风险，描绘过于温馨的画面。它们不是泰迪熊，仍是野生动物。”谢尔曼警告，熊与人类不应过于亲近。“爱熊的一部分在于建立健康界限，并确保它们在不可避免经过我们社区时能成功应对，”他说。通过Instagram账号@poolbearlife，戈登和马丁内斯希望提高人们对如何在熊周围安全行事及如何减少意外相遇的认识。他们强调，他们与黑熊的关系并非某种

这未必是放之四海而皆准的。“这对我们、对我们生活的地方有效，”戈登说。“关键在于找到与野生动物共存的平衡点——我们怎样才能共同繁荣？”马丁内斯说。“我们住在这里，熊也住在这里。我们不想让它们去任何别的地方。”——如需获取关键气候新闻和令人振奋的进展，请订阅《未来地球》时事通讯，而《精华清单》每周两次为您精选专题与见解。欲了解更多BBC科学、技术、环境和健康报道，请在Facebook和Instagram上关注我们。地球 野生动物 自然与户外 环境 热浪 专题 熊

readings.title: Feeling unseen by your boss? Here’s what you can do
body: Feeling unseen by your boss? Here’s what you can do

Ever have your hard work — including your successes — go unnoticed by your manager? Fixable , TED’s new podcast, is here to do just that — to fix the problems of everyday people who call in with their work woes.

In episode four , cohosts and top leadership coaches Frances Frei and Anne Morriss got to know Nai’a, a caller who struggled with receiving recognition after a major reorganization paired her with a new and preoccupied boss. Nai’a was going above and beyond to do her job well, but the lack of acknowledgement and encouragement — and even awareness — of her work was causing her to lose motivation.
Frances’s and Anne’s first piece of advice to Nai’a was simple: See the humanness of what’s going on — and of your manager.

“Sometimes the barrier to showing up as a great collaborator with your manager can be that there’s still some residual frustration about the situation,” Anne explained. “But that emotion is not going to be useful to you.”
Instead, they encouraged Nai’a to recognize the humanity of her manager and forgive them for making mistakes.
Frances and Anne also shared this strategy with her to practice: Choose curiosity over judgment.

Here’s how Frances put it: “You have a choice between judgment and curiosity, because both can’t exist at the same time. So if you have judgment about your manager, you can’t really be curious about their situation. And when you’re thinking of your manager as a person who’s got a lot of part-time jobs, how do we set them up for success?”

“The simplest expression of curiosity — which is truly a magical elixir in a workplace — is in the form of questions,” said Anne. For example, you could start by asking your manager what process works best for them to learn about your accomplishments and contributions. Or, you could focus on how you can make your meetings with them more productive by asking them, “How can our one-on-one time be of service to what we’re trying to achieve together?”

Another option: Be open about your concerns, and ask your manager what their vision of your success looks like. You could say something like, “Here’s my fear: I’m working really hard, and in this state of flux, I’m afraid that six months will go by and people are going to wonder whether or not I did a good job. So it’s just helpful for me to be clear — what is a good job and how can I help in getting that data for you?”

Across industries and across the world, many people are going through workplace reorganizations and other sweeping changes. And like Nai’a, it’s normal to feel anxious and stressed by what’s happening and to need to go through a readjustment period. Leading with questions — and seeing your boss as another human you’re collaborating with — can help you gain back some agency and autonomy.

“Try doing what you can, and marvel at how the other person changes as a result, as opposed to coming up with the list of how you would like the other person to change,” said Frances. “I think you’re going to be pleasantly surprised; that’s the beautiful part of this.”

No matter your job or business, you’ll find actionable advice on Fixable that can improve your workdays. In other episodes, learn how to overcome communication roadblocks, scale up your side project and lead more productive meetings. Plus: Click here for a chance to get your own work question answered on the show! Listen to Fixable now wherever you get your podcasts.
About the author Hayley Caldwell is a copywriter on the Audience Development team at TED.

##段落
感觉老板没看见你？这里有一些你可以做的事  
 2023年6月15日  
 /  
 海莉·考德威尔  
 Facebook  
 X

 你是否曾经觉得自己的努力工作——包括你的成功——没有被经理注意到？TED的新播客《Fixable》正是为此而来——帮助那些带着职场烦恼打进电话的普通人解决问题。

##段落
在第四集中，联合主持人兼顶级领导力教练弗朗西丝·弗雷和安妮·莫里斯认识了一位来电者奈阿，她在一次大规模重组后与一位新上任且心不在焉的老板搭档，难以获得认可。奈阿为了把工作做好付出了超出预期的努力，但缺乏认可、鼓励——甚至缺乏对她工作的关注——让她逐渐失去动力。

##段落
弗朗西丝和安妮给奈阿的第一条建议很简单：看清事情的“人性面”——也要看清你经理的“人性面”。

##段落
“有时候，与经理成为优秀合作伙伴的障碍，可能源于你对现状仍残留的一些挫败感，”安妮解释说。“但那种情绪对你没有任何用处。”

##段落
相反，她们鼓励奈阿去理解经理作为人的一面，并原谅他们犯错。

##段落
弗朗西丝和安妮还与奈阿分享了一个可以练习的策略：选择好奇，而非评判。

##段落
弗朗西丝是这样说的：“你在评判和好奇之间做选择，因为两者无法同时存在。所以如果你对经理有评判，你就无法真正对他们的处境感到好奇。而当你把经理看作一个身兼多职的人时，我们该如何帮助他们走向成功？”

##段落
“好奇最简单的一种表达——它其实是职场中的神奇灵药——就是提问的形式，”安妮说。例如，你可以先问问经理，他们最希望通过什么方式来了解你的成绩和贡献。或者，你也可以专注于如何让你们的会议更高效，比如问他们：“我们的一对一时间怎样才能更好地服务于我们共同想实现的目标？”

##段落
另一个选择：坦诚说出你的担忧，并询问经理，他们眼中你的成功是什么样子。你可以这样说：“我的担忧是：我非常努力地工作，但在这种变动不定的状态下，我担心六个月过去后，大家会怀疑我是否把工作做好了。所以对我来说，明确标准很有帮助——什么是‘做得好’，以及我能怎样帮你收集这些信息？”

##段落
在全世界各行各业中，许多人正在经历职场重组和其他大规模变革。和奈阿一样，面对正在发生的事情感到焦虑和压力，并需要经历一段重新调整的时期，都是正常的。

以提问的方式与老板互动——把老板视为与你协作的另一个普通人——能帮你重获一些主动权和自主性。

“试着做你能做的，然后惊讶于对方因此发生的变化，而不是列出一堆你希望对方如何改变的清单，”弗朗西斯说。“我觉得你会惊喜的；这正是这件事的美好之处。”

无论你从事什么工作或经营什么业务，你都能在《Fixable》中找到改善工作日的实用建议。在其他集数中，学习如何克服沟通障碍、扩大你的副业规模，以及主持更高效的会议。另外：点击此处，有机会让你的工作问题在节目中获答！现在就收听《Fixable》，无论你从哪里获取播客。

readings.title: A federal judge just discovered a whole new way to place ICE above the law
body: Politics A federal judge just discovered a whole new way to place ICE above the law ﻿Texas is where MAGA goes to escape the rule of law. by Ian Millhiser Sep 1, 2026, 4:25 PM UTC Gift ICE agents depart the Bishop Henry Whipple Federal Building on February 4, 2026 in Minneapolis. John Moore/Getty Images Ian Millhiser is a senior correspondent at Vox, where he focuses on the Supreme Court, the Constitution, and the decline of liberal democracy in the United States. He received a JD from Duke University and is the author of two books on the Supreme Court. For a brief moment last week, it appeared that an ICE officer, who allegedly shot a man during the early 2026 occupation of Minneapolis and then lied about it, might actually face legal consequences for his actions. Christian Castro, the now-suspended ICE officer in question, was confined to a Texas jail and potentially faced two sets of criminal charges. Minnesota prosecutors charged him with four felony counts of assault and one count of falsely reporting a crime, and sought his extradition from Texas, where he ordinarily lives , to Minnesota. Federal prosecutors, meanwhile, were reportedly planning to charge Castro with a criminal violation of a federal civil rights law . Email (required) Sign Up By submitting your email, you agree to our Terms and Privacy Notice . This site is protected by reCAPTCHA and the Google Privacy Policy and Terms of Service apply. Castro’s case was on track to become an encouraging example of how the American system can bring rogue law enforcement officers to account — a federal officer facing clear consequences for allegedly breaking the law in the unpopular and violent wave of ICE raids in Minnesota . But all of that now appears to be in limbo. According to the New York Times, the federal charges, which had to be approved by officials in Washington, DC, “ fell apart in the final hours for reasons that remain unclear .” Castro, meanwhile, may never return to Minnesota — and may even flee to Mexico — thanks to a federal court decision permitting Texas’s Republican Gov. Greg Abbott to effectively sit on Minnesota’s request to extradite Castro until after a state law required Castro’s release. It’s the latest chapter in an ongoing saga where Trump administration officials, federal courts eager to shield federal law enforcement officers from justice , and now Texas state officials all work together to ensure that ICE and other law enforcement personnel involved in Trump’s violent crackdown in Minnesota face no legal consequences for their actions. If Castro gets off scot-free, he will owe his freedom to an unusual combination of federal and state officials who appear to have taken extraordinary measures to shield Castro from accountability. But while his case is unusually dramatic, it is hardly unique. An array of MAGA sympathizers and movement conservatives in state governments, the federal judiciary, and the Trump administration have all pushed to place ICE and similar agencies above the law. Castro allegedly fired his gun through the door of Julio Sosa-Celis’s Minneapolis home in January, striking him in the leg. Although the Trump administration initially claimed that Sosa-Celis and his roommate attacked ICE officers with a broom and shovel, that allegation fell apart after prosecutors viewed video of the incident . Castro was suspended from his job at ICE without pay. In May, a Minnesota prosecutor filed charges against Castro, and Castro was later arrested in Texas pursuant to an arrest warrant arising out of those charges. That arrest should have guaranteed that Castro would be returned to Minnesota for trial. The Constitution provides that “a Person charged in any State with Treason, Felony, or other Crime, who shall flee from Justice, and be found in another State, shall on Demand of the executive Authority of the State from which he fled, be delivered up , to be removed to the State having Jurisdiction of the Crime.” Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz formally sought Castro’s extradition on June 2. Rather than comply with this request, however, Abbott took two actions that may prevent Castro from ever being tried for his alleged crimes. Abbott initiated an investigation, claiming, on dubious legal grounds , that he may not be able to extradite Castro because Castro does not meet the legal definition of a “fugitive.” Abbott also sent his lawyers to federal court to argue that the court could not order Texas to comply with the Constitution’s mandatory extradition provision. Meanwhile, a deadline loomed over Minnesota’s request. Though Castro was incarcerated in a Texas jail, Texas law only permitted the jail to hold Castro for 90 days , at least without an order from Abbott saying that Castro must be extradited. During his incarceration, Castro also made several phone calls to his romantic partner in Mexico, and they discussed Castro’s desire to move to that country. So Minnesota quite reasonably feared that, if the 90 days were allowed to expire, Castro would flee the country. Nevertheless, last Wednesday a Trump-appointed Judge Fernando Rodriguez Jr. backed Abbott’s play. His opinion in Walz v. Abbott rests on an extraordinarily credulous interpretation of Abbott’s treatment of Castro. Briefly, Rodriguez’s opinion claims that it is too soon for a court to order Abbott to extradite Castro because Abbott has not yet formally “denied the request for a rendition warrant.” Instead, Rodriguez notes that Abbott asked Texas’s secretary of state to investigate whether Castro should be surrendered to Minnesota, and suggests that Minnesota must wait for that “investigation” to play out. Oddly, Rodriguez’s opinion also includes a footnote indicating that he believes Abbott’s supposed investigation is baseless . The premise of that investigation is that Castro may not count as a “fugitive” because he moved to Texas after ICE directed him to do so. But, as Rodriguez notes, the Supreme Court defined who counts as a fugitive more than a century ago, and the Court’s definition does not exclude people who move because of a job, federal or otherwise. So, to summarize Rodriguez’s decision, he ruled that Texas may delay complying with Minnesota’s extradition request, based on an investigation into a legal question that the Supreme Court has already resolved, and that it may delay compliance until state law requires Texas to release Castro. Castro was released on Thursday. Thanks to this decision, it is now unclear whether Castro will ever face charges. Even if he remains in Texas, and even if Abbott eventually decides to comply with the extradition request, Texas authorities will now have to find Castro again and rearrest him. And Castro may flee to Mexico. While Minnesota can formally request Castro’s extradition from Mexico, that process could take years . And, in case there is any doubt, there’s now strong evidence that Abbott’s “investigation” was a sham, and that Abbott was always motivated by hostility toward Minnesota’s attempt to prosecute Castro. One day after Rodriguez issued his decision, Abbott posted on X mocking Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison , which said that Ellison and his legal team “are such bad lawyers.” The post also labeled Minnesota a “sanctuary state” and threatened to bus immigrants from Texas to Minnesota. Even if Castro had been delivered to Minnesota authorities without incident, or even if he is arrested in Minnesota at some point in the future, it’s far from clear whether state prosecutors may bring charges against a federal law enforcement officer who allegedly violated Minnesota’s criminal law while carrying out his official duties. And the biggest obstacle standing against such a prosecution is a fairly sensible Supreme Court decision that long predates modern political fights over immigration enforcement. The Court’s decision in In re Neagle (1890) arose from a wild incident where a former chief justice of the state of California attempted to kill a sitting Supreme Court justice. David Terry, the former state justice, married a woman who claimed that she was entitled to a share of a US senator’s fortune. After Justice Stephen Field ruled against Terry’s wife, Terry threatened Field’s life, and so Field was assigned a deputy US Marshal named David Neagle as his bodyguard. Some time after Field’s decision against Terry’s wife, the justice was traveling by train in California, and he was attacked by Terry. Neagle shot and killed Terry. And California attempted to charge Neagle, the federal bodyguard, with murder. The Supreme Court tossed out this prosecution, and that decision has long been read to limit state governments’ power to prosecute federal officers who commit a state law crime while engaged in their official duties. That said, the Court’s more recent decision in Martin v. United States (2025) suggests that Neagle may not be a total bar to state prosecutions of ICE officers. Martin read Neagle fairly narrowly, to say that federal officials are protected from state prosecutions only when their actions “were ‘necessary and proper’ in the discharge of their federal responsibilities.” So that suggests that, if Castro is tried for violating Minnesota law, the question of whether he is immune from prosecution is likely to turn on whether courts determine that his alleged decision to fire a shot through Sosa-Celis’s door (and, potentially, to lie about Sosa-Celis’s actions) was a “necessary and proper” way for Castro to carry out his responsibilities as an immigration enforcement officer. It’s hard to predict, however, how the courts would rule on this question. The Martin decision is fairly new, and the rule Martin seems to apply to federal officers charged with state crimes is vague. Federal law also provides that Castro’s trial, should it happen, must occur in federal court — although this federal court may still hear a state-law prosecution. And that means that any decision allowing Castro’s prosecution to move forward would appeal to the US Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit, which is one of the most conservative appeals courts in the federal system . Of course, if Minnesota lost in the Eighth Circuit, it could potentially bring the question of whether Castro may be charged with violating a Minnesota criminal law to the Supreme Court. But, while the Martin decision suggests that Minnesota may have a chance of prevailing before the justices, several of the Court’s other precedents indicate that this Court is unlikely to rule against a federal law enforcement officer. Separately from the legal question of whether someone like Castro can be charged with a crime, there is also the question of whether the victim could sue. It used to be the case that people who are victimized by federal law enforcement officers could sue those officers directly, but the current Supreme Court has virtually shut down these suits. The Court’s treatment of this question is a window into their expansive view of immunity for federal law enforcement. More than five decades ago, the Supreme Court established in Bivens v. Six Unknown Names Agents (1971) that federal officers who violate the Fourth Amendment’s ban on “unreasonable searches and seizures” may be sued and potentially ordered to compensate their victim. But the Court’s current majority is extremely hostile to Bivens , and has walked right up to the edge of overruling it. In Hernández v. Mesa (2020), the Court’s Republican majority held that a Border Patrol agent who allegedly fatally shot a Mexican teenager in the face was immune from a lawsuit brought by the teenager’s family. More recently, in Egbert v. Boule (2022), the Court declared that federal law enforcement officers are immune from suit if there is “any rational reason (even one)” to justify giving them immunity. In November, the Court will hear the Nielsen v. Watanabe that could potentially overrule what little remains of Bivens . The Supreme Court’s Republican majority, in other words, has spent the last several years immunizing federal law enforcement officers like Castro from civil lawsuits. That doesn’t necessarily mean that it will also immunize Castro from criminal charges brought under state law, should his case somehow wind up before the justices, but it isn’t a hopeful sign for Minnesota prosecutors. And that’s, of course, assuming that Minnesota law enforcement somehow manages to take custody of Castro. Abbott’s gamesmanship, and Rodriguez’s decision to bless that gamesmanship, may ultimately mean that Castro is never apprehended by Minnesota officials. ##段落
政治：一名联邦法官刚刚发现了一种全新的方式，将ICE置于法律之上。得克萨斯州是MAGA逃避法治的避风港。作者：Ian Millhiser，2026年9月1日，下午4:25 UTC。赠阅：2026年2月4日，ICE特工离开明尼阿波利斯的毕晓普·亨利·惠普尔联邦大楼。图片来源：John Moore/Getty Images。Ian Millhiser是Vox的高级记者，专注于最高法院、宪法以及美国自由民主的衰落。他拥有杜克大学的法学博士学位，并撰写了两本关于最高法院的著作。

##段落
上周短暂时刻，一名ICE官员据称在2026年初占领明尼阿波利斯期间开枪射杀一名男子并随后撒谎，看似可能因其行为面临法律后果。涉案的Christian Castro，这位目前被停职的ICE官员，被关押在得克萨斯州的一所监狱，并可能面临两套刑事指控。明尼苏达州检察官指控他四项重罪攻击罪和一项虚假报告罪，并寻求将他从通常居住的得克萨斯州引渡至明尼苏达州。同时，据报道，联邦检察官计划以违反联邦民权法的刑事罪名起诉Castro。

##段落
电子邮件（必填）注册。提交您的电子邮件即表示您同意我们的条款和隐私声明。本网站受reCAPTCHA保护，并适用Google隐私政策和服务条款。Castro的案件原本有望成为美国体系如何追究流氓执法官员责任的鼓舞人心的例子——一名联邦官员因涉嫌在明尼苏达州不受欢迎且暴力的ICE突袭浪潮中违法而面临明确后果。但这一切现在似乎陷入僵局。据《纽约时报》报道，原本必须由华盛顿特区官员批准的联邦指控“在最后时刻因尚不明确的原因而瓦解”。与此同时，由于一项联邦法院裁决允许得克萨斯州共和党州长Greg Abbott有效地搁置明尼苏达州引渡Castro的请求，直到州法律要求释放Castro，他可能永远不会返回明尼苏达州，甚至可能逃往墨西哥。

##段落
这是持续事件中的最新篇章：特朗普政府官员、急于保护联邦执法官员免受司法追究的联邦法院，以及现在的得克萨斯州官员，共同协作，确保参与特朗普在明尼苏达州暴力镇压的ICE及其他执法人员不会因其行为面临法律后果。如果Castro逍遥法外，他将把自己的自由归功于联邦和州官员的异常结合，这些官员似乎采取了非常措施来保护Castro免受问责。但尽管他的案件异常特殊，它已成为一个更广泛问题的鲜明象征：美国法治体系在政治压力下日益脆弱，执法问责制正被系统性侵蚀。

虽然这一事件本身具有戏剧性，但它并非独一无二。州政府、联邦司法系统以及特朗普政府中的众多MAGA同情者和运动保守派都在推动将ICE及类似机构置于法律之上。据称，卡斯特罗在1月份透过胡里奥·索萨-塞利斯的明尼阿波利斯家中的门开枪，击中了他的腿部。尽管特朗普政府最初声称索萨-塞利斯及其室友用扫帚和铁锹袭击了ICE官员，但检察官查看事件视频后，这一指控不攻自破。卡斯特罗被ICE停职，无薪停职。5月，明尼苏达州检察官对卡斯特罗提起指控，卡斯特罗随后根据这些指控引发的逮捕令在得克萨斯州被捕。这次逮捕本应确保卡斯特罗被送回明尼苏达州接受审判。宪法规定：“凡在任何一州被控犯有叛国罪、重罪或其他罪行的人，若逃避司法追究并在另一州被找到，应根据其逃出州行政当局的要求将其移交，以便送往对犯罪有管辖权的州。”明尼苏达州州长蒂姆·沃尔兹于6月2日正式请求引渡卡斯特罗。然而，阿博特并未遵从这一请求，反而采取了两项行动，可能阻止卡斯特罗因其涉嫌的罪行而受审。阿博特启动了一项调查，并基于可疑的法律理由声称，他可能无法引渡卡斯特罗，因为卡斯特罗不符合“逃犯”的法律定义。阿博特还派律师前往联邦法院，辩称法院不能命令得克萨斯州遵守宪法强制性的引渡条款。与此同时，明尼苏达州的请求面临一个紧迫的最后期限。尽管卡斯特罗被关押在得克萨斯州的监狱中，但得克萨斯州法律仅允许监狱将卡斯特罗关押90天，至少在阿博特没有下令必须引渡卡斯特罗的情况下如此。在监禁期间，卡斯特罗还多次打电话给他在墨西哥的恋人，讨论了他移居该国的愿望。因此，明尼苏达州非常合理地担心，如果90天期限届满，卡斯特罗会逃离该国。然而，上周三，特朗普任命的法官小费尔南多·罗德里格斯支持了阿博特的策略。他在“沃尔兹诉阿博特案”中的意见基于对阿博特处理卡斯特罗方式的极其轻信的解释。简而言之，罗德里格斯的意见声称，法院命令阿博特引渡卡斯特罗还为时过早，因为阿博特尚未正式“拒绝引渡令请求”。相反，罗德里格斯指出，阿博特已要求得克萨斯州州务卿调查是否应将卡斯特罗移交明尼苏达州，并暗示米

明尼苏达州必须等待那场“调查”结束。奇怪的是，罗德里格斯的意见中还包含一个脚注，表明他认为阿博特所谓的调查毫无根据。该调查的前提是，卡斯特罗可能不算“逃犯”，因为他在ICE指示他这样做后搬到了得克萨斯州。但是，正如罗德里格斯所指出的，最高法院在一个多世纪前就定义了谁算逃犯，而法院的定义并不排除因工作（无论是联邦工作还是其他工作）而搬迁的人。因此，总结罗德里格斯的裁决，他裁定得克萨斯州可以推迟遵守明尼苏达州的引渡请求，理由是对一个最高法院已经解决的

##段落
在加利福尼亚乘坐火车时，他遭到特里袭击。尼格尔开枪打死了特里。加利福尼亚州试图以谋杀罪起诉联邦保镖尼格尔。最高法院驳回了这一起诉，该判决长期以来被视为限制州政府起诉在执行公务期间犯下州法律罪行的联邦官员的权力。尽管如此，最高法院在马丁诉美国案（2025）中的最新判决表明，尼格尔案可能并非完全阻止州起诉移民海关执法局官员。马丁案对尼格尔案的解读相当狭窄，认为联邦官员只有在行动“对于履行其联邦职责是‘必要且适当’的”时，才受保护免于州起诉。因此，这意味着如果卡斯特罗因违反明尼苏达州法律而受审，他是否免于起诉的问题很可能取决于法院是否认定他涉嫌决定向索萨-塞利斯的门开枪（以及可能撒谎关于索萨-塞利斯的行动）是卡斯特罗履行其移民执法官员职责的“必要且适当”方式。然而，很难预测法院将如何裁决这一问题。马丁案的判决相当新，马丁案似乎适用于被控犯有州罪行的联邦官员的规则也很模糊。联邦法律还规定，卡斯特罗的审判（如果发生）必须在联邦法院进行——尽管该联邦法院仍可审理州法律起诉。这意味着任何允许卡斯特罗起诉推进的裁决都将上诉至美国第八巡回上诉法院，该法院是联邦系统中最为保守的上诉法院之一。当然，如果明尼苏达州在第八巡回法院败诉，它有可能将卡斯特罗是否可以被控违反明尼苏达州刑法的问题提交至最高法院。但是，尽管马丁案的判决表明明尼苏达州在法官面前可能有机会获胜，最高法院的其他几项先例表明，该法院不太可能作出不利于联邦执法官员的裁决。除了像卡斯特罗这样的人是否可以被控犯罪这一法律问题之外，还存在受害者能否提起诉讼的问题。过去，遭受联邦执法官员侵害的人可以直接起诉这些官员，但现任最高法院几乎已经关闭了此类诉讼的大门。法院对此问题的处理方式，让我们得以窥见其对联邦执法官员豁免权的宽泛看法。五十多年前，最高法院在比文斯诉六名未知特工案（1971）中确立，违反第四修正案禁止不合理搜查和扣押的联邦官员可以被起诉。

关于"不合理搜查和扣押"的诉讼可能被提起，并可能被命令赔偿受害者。但最高法院目前的多数派对Bivens案极为敌视，并且已经走到了推翻它的边缘。在Hernández诉Mesa案（2020年）中，法院的共和党多数派裁定，一名据称开枪打死一名墨西哥少年脸部的边境巡逻人员免于该少年家属提起的诉讼。更近期，在Egbert诉Boule案（2022年）中，法院宣布，如果有"任何合理理由（哪怕只有一个）"来证明给予联邦执法人员豁免权是合理的，他们就免于诉讼。11月，法院将审理Nielsen诉Watanabe案，该案可能推翻Bivens案仅存的一点内容。换句话说，最高法院的共和党多数派在过去几年中一直在让像Castro这样的联邦执法人员免于民事诉讼。这不一定意味着，如果他的案件最终呈现在法官面前，他们也会让Castro免于根据州法律提起的刑事指控，但这对明尼苏达州的检察官来说并不是一个乐观的信号。当然，这还假设明尼苏达州的执法部门能设法将Castro拘留。Abbott的策略游戏，以及Rodriguez决定支持这种策略游戏，最终可能意味着Castro永远不会被明尼苏达州官员逮捕。查看更多：刑事司法 移民政策 政治 最高法院 美国联邦法院 一名联邦法官刚刚发现了一种全新的方式，让ICE凌驾于法律之上 用最新的Vox填字游戏让大脑休息一下 最高法院最糟糕的想法之一可能让中期选举免受特朗普的影响 最高法院刚刚给了特朗普他的非法舞厅 真正阻止数据中心需要什么？电子邮件（必填）注册 提交您的电子邮件即表示您同意我们的条款和隐私声明。本网站受reCAPTCHA保护，并适用Google隐私政策和服务条款。广告客户内容 来自 这是原生广告的标题
